Thank you, Sir. I probably am not very well acquainted with Parliamentary procedure. He used to sit in this House; but what he said struck me as a warning, and I cannot see where we are drifting unless into a desperate situation which we cannot get out of. If I may be pardoned for using personalities, I am one who has been willing to go into things very deeply, to hypothecate every particle of property that I have when I could see with my optics a thing that was not too speculative, and in the different contingencies that have come up, I have had to sweat to get out. The Government is getting into that debt from which I see no way out unless we have an enormous immigration into this country and a tremendous production.
The Government owns praatioally ithe whole press of this country. Why have they not asked the press to drive the facts home to the people of Canada that we must have production from the soil? We know very well that timber is a quick asset, and that ' farm lands give an annual crop. Now if the people had been prevailed on to go back on the land and produce, we should have had something with which to pay our
[.Mr. Baldwin.]
national debt. Let me warn the Government and all those within sound of my voice, that a year from now food stuffs will cost more than they do to-day. Eggs, when they can be got, are going into cold storage at fifty cents. Butter is more than ten cents higher than a year ago; salt poTk, which can be barrelled and kept for years, is now $70 a barrel. Everything made of fats has gone up. Soap is jumping and will probably be as high in this country in a year or two as the boys had to pay for it in France, and 'that is a tremendous price.
There is no way out except, to use the words of the Minister of Finance, to produce and save. I prefer the more homely expression " work " We never shall be able to pay our national debt by working only six hours a day. After the American war the people of that country went into farming in a most- extensive way. They did not build up any navy; foreign powers did their carrying trade. Farm lands were taken up right to the foot of the Rockies, the population increased tremendously, and the United States became a great manufacturing country. And then they commenced to build a navy, but not a very big one until after the war started. Canada is in a very bad environment because we are living next to a populous and rich nation, and we are acquiring the habit of spending money and spending it needlessly. If this poor country was back in the position it was in fifty or sixty years ago we would be in a much better position to pay our debt than we are to-day. We have taken on the burdens of a rich people. Look at the automobiles in this country to-day. Look at the money that is being spent in the playhouses. The United States closed up their amusement houses during the war, but nothing of that kind was done in Canada.
In this country, I am told, we have only 185 people to every mile of railway, which is *a greater mileage according to population probably than any other country in the world, and yet-I do not want to insult the West-the people of the West are coming down here and asking for railways into every squaw settlement and back region. Other people are talking about aeroplanes to go to the moon, the North Pole, the Yukon, and everywhere else. Let us come to our senses as loyal patriotic Canadians and realize that we have got to buckle down to work, economize, and save. There is no harm in my saying that, because the great banks of this country have issued letters warning people against buying too many new clothes, and when those letters were issued the clothes which cost twenty

dollars are probably costing forty dollars now. The saving of forty dollars by a million people means a national saving of forty million dollars. Every one knows that all of us, both men and women, have more clothing than we need. In olden times clothes were worn to protect the body, and not for show.

Has any country in the
world a greater railroad mileage per capita than Canada?	[DOT]

Although I have
travelled somewhat I am afraid I cannot answer that question. My hon. friend should put his question to the Minister of Railways. I think, however, that my statement as to railway mileage in this country is correct. I was going on to say that a policy of work and save will save this country. We must economize and do the things that go with it. There must be a better feeling among the people. We have got to make ourselves a people who will extend a cordial helping hand. We must extend good cheer and the brightness of our nature to improve the appalling state of affairs in this country to-day. It seems to me it is worse than a disease, or an epidemic. I believe that this Government has got a "tremendous burden upon its shoulders. Now is the accepted time and the day of salvation-not the day for procrastination. If commissions are going to do the work of the Government I would suggest that we amend our constitution. Our representation in this House is based upon the population of Quebec, and I would suggest that Quebec send a member to this House from each judicial district. That would reduce the membership of this House by two-thirds. If this country is going to be run by commissions and Orders in Council, if Orders in Council are going to do the work which the elected representatives of the people are sent here to do, the adoption of my suggestion would mean a big saving to the country.
I remarked in this House some months ago, that I thought the Cabinet should be reduced by two-thirds, and if necessary have bureaus to help them along. I do not hear any hon. members cheering that suggestion, so I think it is fair to assume that it will not be acted upon.	_
I hope the War Measures Act will be dispensed with as speedily as possible and that its provisions will be resorted to no longer. I think that the Franchise Act is the cause of the unrest in Canada today. Indeed, I think it is largely responsible for the gravest features of the unrest, and the Government should introduce as early as possible a franchise measure that will give to every man who has not committed any act of violence in this country, and who in the past has exercised the franchise, the right to vote. This right should not be based upon any racial line of de-marfcation, but should be within the reach of every citizen who commits no breach of law. I am as much a supporter of law and order as any other hon. member of this House, and I am just as ready to see those punished who commit acts of violence and merit punishment. The Franchise Act should foe based on the provincial lists. It would be less expensive to the country and would be fair. Municipalities prepare those lists and know just who should vote.
In regard to the housing question, I believe that this matter is wrong in every respect. It is not going to help the people in the rural sections, and they are the people whom we want to help. The farmers and poor people of the country need assistance, and I advocated last year the establishment of national reserve banks by means of Which a farmer could secure a certain amount of money, two-thirds say, of the equity in his estate'. I observe that an eminent authority, a banker of high standing, recently expressed the opinion that there should be national reserve banks in Canada.
As regards roads, I think the sum of $25,000,000 has been set aside for the improvement of highways. This is a matter that appeals very strongly to every one who lives in a rural section. Cities can connect with one another only by way of the country, and this question is therefore important to people in the country. What struck me as a notable fact was that the members from Ontario said that for every dollar that was appropriated in this project only 65 cents went into the road, while 35 cents went somewhere else. This is not true in the case of the province from which I come, where everything was done that was possible and every cent expended went on the highways and not into somebody's pocket. While I am on this subject, let me say that the roads and public works of Canada should provide means of employment for every criminal from every jail and penitentiary and internment camp in the country. In other words, every man who is fed and clothed by the Dominion of Canada should work for the Dominion. This is a most opportune time, now that the returned soldier is back in

the country, to put this proposal into effect. France adopted this system many years ago, and I think the United States recently adopted it, with great success in both cases. It is intolerable that native-born Canadians or those who have become citizens by adoption should work for and support criminals and keep them in idleness in aggregations, while they might with profit to themselves be doing work that would fit them to be better citizens at the expiration of their terms of imprisonment, I heartily advocate this system and trust that it will be adopted. It is not too much to expect that those who have violated the law should pay for their keep. This is only common sense and must appeal to every thinking person. Why, even the honey bees kill the drones, for they will not support non-producers, and it would be better for the criminals and for the country as well if such men were put to useful and profitable work. We could move them from one section of the country to another in order that they might be employed the year round. They could be sent to British Columbia in winter and could be put to work in the East in summer. Altogether I think it is time that we should take this proposal into consideration.
Quebec, a province of which I am most proud, has saved the Dominion of Canada on two or three occasions, and it is saving it now. This is evidenced by the fact that there is practically no unrest at the present time in that great province, which can support and sustain tens of millions of inhabitants with its great water-powers, its great valleys and. great rivers. No trouble exists in that province. There are settlements, sixty and eighty miles up rivers, establishing new parishes. Yet they are not rushing into Parliament for public money to drain lands and build railroads. The people are happy and content in Quebec, and they are tolerant, just, and right in their relations with the minority. Under Sir Lomer Gouin, we 'have a government of which we are justly proud, and it is a revelation to compare the state of finance in Quebec with that as revealed in this Parliament. In that wonderful province there are water-powers enough to drive all the industries and to pull every railway train that will ever go through that part of the country, and the possibilities in the future are untold. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have occupied sufficient time in view of the fact that it is pretty well understood on both sides of 
the House that it is desirable that the House should adjourn before very long.

Mr. Speaker, in my few remarks this evening I shall attempt to emulate the Minister of Customs in his brevity, although I do not hope to follow his example to the extent of concluding in fifteen minutes. However, I shall endeavour to finish in about twice that time. In that brief space I shall not attempt to decide that century-old question as to whether free trade or protection is the best policy for any country, because the greatest intellects in England have been pondering that question for the past hundred years, and have not yet by any means decided it. In fact, they are starting the discussion all over again.
In regard to the Budget which the Minister of Finance delivered in this House so ably a few days ago, I am confident that it will not satisfy the extremists on either side of the House or in the country. Neither the extreme free traders nor the extreme protectionists will be satisfied with the result, but I believe that the average citizen of Canada, when he takes into consideration the fact that Canada owes pretty nearly $2,000,000,000 instead of $330,000,000 as before the war; that $115,000,000 in interest has to be raised; and that a sum between $35,000,000 and $40,000,000 has to be provided for pensions, when he thinks of the vast problems which will have to be dealt with, he will regard the Budget as fairly satisfactory.
I believe that the average citizen will be particularly pleased with the fact that the Government has taken that extra seven and a half per cent off the necessaries of life. He will also feel satisfied that the income tax has been increased and will be gratified with the promise of the Finance Minister that a revision of the tariff shall be made within the next year. I presume the average citizen will understand that the revision referred to is not a revision upwards. The other day when the debate took place here regarding the unrest in the country I attempted to get the floor on two or three occasions, but I was not fortunate enough to catch your eye, Mr. Speaker. I therefore am now going to say a few words on that subject for the reason that my own city, among many of the cities in the West, is one of the centres of unrest at the present time. I think, Mr. Speaker, that when you take into consideration the vast problems that this Government has handled, and the fair manner on the whole in which they

have been dealt with; when you take into account the fact that we have just finished a great war in which the Allies were victorious-a victory which was partly won by the Canadians-I think it is a fair question to ask why is unrest so prominent in this country? Why is Canada tc-day in such an appalling condition of unrest? If you treat a sickness or malady, whether it be in a human being or in a nation, it is necessary to find the cause; otherwise, you cannot treat that malady intelligently; and until you remove the cause you cannot cure the disease. I should say there are three main causes for the prevailing unrest in this country. The first-perhaps not the most important, but the first-I would attribute to the highstrung condition of the people of the world, due to the mental and physical strain through which they have gone by reason of the recent war. I believe I am safe in saying that none of us is absolutely normal in his mental actions at the present moment. In other words, we are more or less irritable in our mental actions and reactions to-day. That I would put as one of the causes of the prevailing unrest in Canada. The second cause, and a very important one, is the almost prohibitive cost of the necessaries of life; and the third cause, I would say, is that there are in this country a number of agitators, influenced by not the fairest of motives, who are using those other two conditions to stir up trouble.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as to the reasons for the high cost of living: I would place first, and most important in the list, the fact that in the recent war forty or fifty millions of men throughout the world were taken from productive processes and placed at destructive processes. In other words, forty or fifty millions of men were taken from productive processes and necessarily allowed to use up the products of the different countries of the world, therefore causing a world shortage of the necessaries of life. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that is perhaps the most important of the causes of the present high cost of living. Second to that I would place the profiteering which has gone on in Canada and in other countries of the world. Now profiteering is not so important a cause of the high cost oi living, but it is to my mind a much more important cause of unrest in Canada. I do not think any man has a right to stand on the floor of this House these days and make the statement that profiteering is going on unless he is prepared to offer some proof that his statement is correct. Therefore, I am going to offer what look 'to me like fairly good proofs that profiteering is going on in the Dominion at the present time. I hold in my hand a letter which was written to the city clerk of Fort William on December 9, six months ago today, by R. J. McFall, " Chief of the High Cost of Living." I cannot help thinking that is a strange title, but that is the way the letter is signed. I shall not read the letter, because I wish to condense my re: marks as much as possible, but in it the writer says that Mr. Crawford, a citizen of Fort William and an accountant by profession, has given him proof of sixteen cases in which the four meat packing houses of that city have overcharged the local consumers in selling meats and such products as butter and eggs to the extent of breaking the law; and he gives forty cases altogether in which he says he can practically supply proof that the packing houses have overcharged the people of Fort William to such an extent that if the city wishes to sue the packing houses and bring them before the courts they can secure a fine of $1,000 in each case, or $40,000 in all; and he advises that the prosecution can be brought under Food Board Order No. 45. He goes on to say that he does not think the retailers are to blame, and that the profits of the packers are dealt with by the Minister of Finance. The question might easily be put up to me that since Mr. McFall has written to the city council suggesting that the meat packers be prosecuted, why has the prosecution not been undertaken? That is a legitimate question, and I am not going to defend the council of Fort William for not doing so except to remark that every city, generally speaking, objects to prosecuting business firms which are carrying on operations within its limits. I think that if the condition of affairs which Mr. McFall has pointed out is to be depended upon, as existing in Fort William it very likely did exist, and does exist now, throughout the country, and it is to my mind the duty of the Government to go ahead and prosecute some of these corporations. I venture to say that if the Government had done that at an early date it would have removed a certain amount of the unrest which now exists.
Another proof that profiteering, to a greater or less extent, is going on in the Dominion, is contained in a report printed in the Toronto Globe, and other papers, of May 25th-the annual financial report of the Dominion Textiles. In that report I read- and I wall condense the statement so as

not to occupy an undue amount of the time of the House-that after all deductions, including $1,100,000 for war and income taxes, a newly-established pension fund, and replacement reserve, there remained for common stock dividend distribution the sum of $1,559,888, or equal to 31.2 per cent against 21.9 per cent in 1917-18 and 15.6 per cent the year before. In other words, in two years the Dominion Textiles Company, which handles the necessaries of life in the form of clothing for the people of this country, doubled their amount of profit and ran it up to 31.2 per cent. I think that is another proof of profiteering in Canada. I do not wish to be unjust to the meat packers referred to in Fort William, or to the Dominion Textiles Company, or ito any other wholesalers or retailers that have been indulging in what we call "profiteering" or making excess profits, because as long as the law permits these companies to make such profits I do not think we can accuse them in a blind, hap-hazard way of doing wrong. These companies, whether wholesale or retail, were organized for the purpose of making money, and that is all they are doing. I presume that if any of the members of the House were shareholders in these companies they would be very pleased to get a high dividend; but the fact remains that such abnormal profits, such examples of profiteering, are one of the causes of the existing unrest.
I'will give what I think is another proof of the profiteering in vogue in Canada in the shape of a statement made by the Hon. Gideon Robertson, Minister of Labour. Hon. Mr. Robertson, when passing through Fort William, gave an interview to the Times-Journal, which has not been contradicted, and therefore may be accepted as being true, in which he says :-
I have enough information before me to assure myself that the jabbers and the retailers are the cause of the high cost of living.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that I have no desire to indulge in destructive criticism in this matter, but I think the Government should interfere, if it is possible for it to do so, in putting a limit to such profits. I may be told that a committee of the House has been appointed to deal with the matter, and I compliment the Government upon appointing that committee, which is a step in the right direction; but I submit that inquiry by committee is rather a slow process, and I think that while the committee is carrying on its work it will be a very wise move for the
fMr, Manion.]
Government, in order to help settle the prevailing unrest, to attempt to limit the excess profits whioii any company is making on the necessaries of life in Canada. I submit also that according to these reports the Government has the information to carry out that suggestion.
Now, Sir, to show that other countries have taken up this question, in 1915 the Government of New Zealand appointed a body called the " Board of Trade." This is from the Canadian Labour Gazette for last month, printed by the Government of Canada, so I take it to be official. This is what the Labour Gazette contains:
A New Zealand statute entitled " The Cost of Living Act 19115," provided for the appointment of a body to be called " The Board of Trade" to investigate and report on conditions of trade, prices, cost of living, etc., in the Dominion of New Zealand. The Minister of Industries and1 Commerce is ex officio president of the Board.	*
*
The Board of Trade decided, under the provisions of the recommendations to devise a scheme for restricting increases in the prices of groceries. Committees of merchants were formed in each of the large centres to advise the Board and to furnish information as to wholesale prices and market conditions.
*
In regard to bacon and ham, owing to a rise in price the Board recommended that export should be prohibited. The meat trade also received considerable attention. Two state meat shops had been set up by the Board in January, 1917, as butchers had refused to keep in force prices approved by the Board.
*
In regard to footwear a scheme was adopted involving an arrangement with the tanners to supply manufacturers of boots with leather at reasonable prices. The Board reported that as a result of the measures taken by the Government and the Board of Trade to stabilize prices, the cost of food had not increased in New Zealand to the same extent as in America.
*
The price of butter sold for consumption in New Zealand was kept lower than the price for export, and the producers for export were made to contribute to an equalization fund to remunerate the producers who sold for home consumption.
I just mention that to show what the Government of New Zealand attempted four years ago to keep down the high cost of living, an attempt which met with some success. I do not believe that any member has a right to offer destructive criticism unless he is prepared to suggest something constructive in its place. It is very easy to tear down; it is very difficult to build up. It is very easy for members to show where the Government have made mistakes and to blame it for any untoward condition in the country. I do not think that is fair unless they are prepared to offer something

constructive in place of it, and I wtish to submit these suggestions along the lines 1 have been speaking of:
First, I suggest that the Government shall take immediate steps to eliminate profiteering of all kinds so far a,s they are able to do so. I may be asked: How is that to be done? There is the question of limiting such people to reasonable profits. Then the difficulty comes up, of course, of deciding what are reasonable profits. The big dealer on a main street with heavy rent and other overhead expenses has to be considered as well as the small dealer off the main street whose expenses are very much less. But governments are appointed to overcome difficulties, and this is not an insuperable difficulty. The New Zealand Government took over the meat shops and obtained control of meat and the other necessaries of life. That is one possible line of action. Then the Minister of Finance gave us some help in his Budget by reducing the tariff on some of the necessaries of life. I would suggest that if later it is found that the high cost of living does not come down, it might be well to consider reducing the tariff still lower on these same necessaries of life. Another measure which 'the New Zealand Government took was to limit export. Many people in this country throw up their hands in horror when any one suggests such a thing. But if no other means are found practicable for bringing down the high cost of living, and the country is getting into a dangerous condition of unrest on account of that high cost of living, any method that is practicable would he wise to try out rather than let the country drift into that dangerous state.
Another suggestion which I have to offer is that we put down the revolutionary of any type. We have been in the habit of always blaming alien enemies. I think that the Government, particularly at the present time, should take into account the fact that a man is a revolutionary, and should ignore his nationality, whether he is a Canadian, an Englishman, a Scotchman, an Irishman or an alien,-treat them all alike. I was struck the other day by a statement made by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton) when coming home from the Peace Conference. He told the soldiers on board ship that it was not essential that any particular [DOT]Government should stay in power in this country or that any particular man or group of men should, but that it was essential that constitutional Government should be upheld. I think that is a principle we [DOT] can all support.
My next suggestion is that the Government should carry on to a still greater extent than in the past-although they have done very good work-efforts for greater co-operation between capital and labour. Unfortunately capital and labour have been antagonists instead of realizing that they are interdependent, and as a result the community has suffered. We should show capital that it is dependent upon labour; and we should show labour that it is dependent upon capital; and we should show both that they are dependent upon the community. By bringing them into cooperation we might possibly settle some of these difficulties. I acknowledge quite frankly the excellent work that Senator Robertson has done to bring about that cooperation.
I appeal to the Government to take up these matters very seriously, and I would not state them on the floor of the House if I did not feel their urgent importance. I am not speaking in any spirit of destructive criticism, hut rather in an effort to offer constructive suggestions, because I think it is very important that we should try to convince the people that we are really sincere in our efforts to bring down the cost of the necessities of life, even if we do not accomplish a great deal in that direction.
I wish to touch on another subject very briefly, and that is the question of the development of our natural resources. Last year I took this question up, particularly in regard to iron, and I pointed out, among other things, that after the war was over raw materials would rule the world of commerce, and that Canada possessed those raw materials in abundance only awaiting the hand of man to develop them. I stated that if you studied the commercial history of the world you found that the commercial development of France, England, the United States or Germany was in direct proportion to the production of pig iron and steel. I said that if Canada was to. take her place among the nations of the world she must develop her natural resources. We have hundreds of millions' of tons of iron ore scattered from the Atlantic to the Pacific, while at the same time we were importing 95 per cent of the iron ore used in our blast furnaces and steel plants. In 1896, 67 per cent of the iron ore used in the blast furnaces and steel plants of Canada was Canadian iron ore. Of course, a much smaller amount was manufactured then. In 1916, twenty years later, it fell from 67 per cent to 11 per cent; in 1917 to 4 per cent, and last year it had gone still

lower. I would like to point out that Quebec produces 90 per cent of the asbestos of the world, Ontario produces 80 per cent of the nickel supply of the world, and the Dominion produces about 15 per cent of the silver. But of iron we produced 93,000 tons and imported well over 2,000,000; in other words, .we used less than 5 per cent of Canadian ore. Last year we imported $6,000,000 worth of iron ore; of iron and steel products including machinery, $155,000,000; oils, $46,000,000; coal, $70,000,000; or a total of $277,000,000. And yet, taking	coal,	there are	in Canada
the heaviest deposits in the world with the exception of those in the United States. Canada takes second place only to the United States in the immensity of her coal deposits. We have over a million million tons in the western and eastern deposits of this country, but unfortunately we have very little in between. In oil we have in Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Peace River District very rich deposits. We have hundreds of millions of tons of iron ore scattered between the Atlantic and the Pacific. We have 19,000,000 horse-power of potential electrical energy in our waterfalls, of which less than 10 per cent has been developed. A short time ago the members of this House heard Stefansson say there were 30,000,009 caribou and 40,000 musk oxen in the Arctic regions of this country ready to be developed into vast meat resources. But attempted oratorical outbursts like mine regarding our natural resources are of no use; unless we develop those resources. I noticed the other day the Finance Minister spoke with some fluency of our vast natural resources. But I repeat, unless we develop them they are of no use to the country. I notice that Mr.. Beatty, the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in a speech delivered in the western country a few days ago, advised the development of these natural resources.
The reasons I give for the development of these natural resources are as follows: In the first plaee, we have in this country forty thousand miles of railway, and more than half of that mileage of these railways are nurselings in the hands of the Government. Canada has one mile of railway for every 190 to 200 people. The member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Butts) put a question in this regard a few moments ago; perhaps this will answer it. The United States has one mile of railway for every 400 people; Great Britain one mile to every
2.000	people and Russia one mile to every
4.000	people. Canada has more railway
['Mr. Manion.]	!	1
mileage than Great Britain with her 45,000,000 people and than France with her 40,000,000 people; and an equal mileage to that of Germany, with its 65,000,000 people. To make our railways catch up with their development we must increase the population and increase the traffic by developing our natural resources.
Another reason why we should develop these resources is that the debt of this country has jumped from $330,000,000 to $2,000,000,000, and our annual interest charges from $15,000,000 to $115,000,000; and our pensions have reached the sum of $35,000,000 or $40,000,000 per annum. The payment of that debt would be assisted to a great extent if we could work out a proper system for the development of these natural resources, and at the same time provide that the nation should share in the profits resulting from that development. For example, Northern Ontario produced during the last twelve years $220,000,000 worth of gold and silver and about $250,000,000 worth of nickel; yet out of that the nation got very little into its coffers. We are continually uttering the fallacy that if we take out of the earth a million dollars in minerals, we have reduced our national debt to 'that extent. But that is not the case, so long as the entire profits resulting from these developments go into the hands of corporations and private individuals. So I believe that we should work out some system for the development of these natural resources akin to what we have done in respect to our water-powers, which we no longer permit to be alienated into the hands of private corporations or individuals. The system need not be one of controlling them entirely; but Canada should get part of the profits.
We have guaranteed credits-and the policy has been criticised in this House- for Roumania, for Belgium, for England, for France. I am not going to quarrel with that policy. There is, perhaps, an element of risk in it; but in times like these, unless we dare something we certainly shall not gain anything. I therefore agree that this policy should be carried into effect, even taking into account the possibility of loss. But why not work out some system in the matter I mention.
Another reason why these natural resources should be developed, particularly the three that I have mentioned, is the fact that oil, coal and iron are all exhaustible materials, and that we import practically all our supplies of these from the United States. In the near future it

may be advisable for the United States, as a matter of self-protection, to shut off the export of some of these minerals to Canada. If that time should come, it would be advisable for Canada to be in a position to produce these natural resources within -the country.
As to concrete proposals for the development of these resources, there are a number of them; I will simply name them without discussing them in detail.
The first is that the Government itself develop these natural resources. Having regard to Canada's debt, it is doubtful whether it would be advisable for us to put millions into a scheme of that sort.
Second, the guaranteeing of the bonds of a private corporation. That procedure has been tried out in Canada fairly well, with not too happy results.
Third, partnership with private corporations, such as the Shell Oil Company's proposition, which was put before the people recently through the press. That principle might work out fairly well, provided, of course, that the basis of the arrangement were not such that the private corporation took all the cream and the country got all the skim-milk. A scheme might be worked out under which the country, in return for giving more or less of an monopoly of a certain area to a corporation, would get a share of the profits.
Fourth, a bonus or bounty system, such as has. been particularly advocated in connection with iron.
Fifth, a thorough investigation into the whole matter. Hon. members, whether protectionists or free-traders, on whichever side of the House they may be, cannot quarrel with a thorough investigation- more thorough than hitherto has been carried out. By the way, our Geological Survey does excellent work. They have their own professional men-men who have taken excellent university courses, but who are being paid the wages, almost, of ordinary labourers. It would be well-spent money if the Government could see its way clear to increase the expenditure on the Mines Department of the Government.
Sixth, and perhaps the best of all, the appointment of a commission or committee of the House to go into the whole question and try to work out some scheme whereby Canada could develop these natural resources. Commissions are unpopular at the present time because there are many, but a committee of the House could be appointed to go into this question, and possibly bring forth some constructive suggestion.
The development of these resources, then, would help to pay our national debt, would increase our population, would increase the home market for our agricultural products, would provide work for our soldiers and for others who desire work, would supply traffic for our over-developed railway system, would increase the prosperity of our country, would make us independent of American raw materials, and, finally, would turn Canada into one of the great commercial countries of the world-always provided, of course, that we can successfully work out a proper scheme to this end. I hope that in the near future, when some of the vast problems now confronting it are solved and set aside, the Government will take up the question of the development of the natural resources of this country.
Hon. H. S. BELAND (Beauce) moved the adjournment of the debate. .

subsubtopic: SPEECH OF SOLICITOR GENERAL MOVING ADOPTION OF REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I move that the House concur in the report of the Special Committee appointed to consider the law in regard to sedition and seditious propaganda presented to the House on Friday last. In making this motion might I be permitted to say in the first place that the recommendations of the Committee are not intended to have any effect whatever upon the recognized labour organizations throughout this country. I think I oan state plainly that the recommendations of the Committee have no such object, and have no such effect. Neither were these recommendations inspired by, nor are they the result of, the Winnipeg strike; the Committee was appointed, and entered upon its duties, before the Winnipeg strike was instituted. I mention this matter on account of an article I saw in the press on Saturday last to the effect that the Special Committee appointed in regard to sedition had brought down a report as a direct result of the strike which existed in Winnipeg, and that the

report might operate adversely upon many labour organizations in Canada. This statement is thoroughly erroneous; the report can have no such operation, and no such effect. It is true that the Committee did look over the whole situation in Canada. It is quite true that the Committee did recognize, what I think must be recognized by every citizen of Canada at the present time, and not only in Canada but in other countries in the world, and that is, that we are to a very large extent at this moment confronted with a new situation, and it will be necessary now and in the future to amend our law, both civil and criminal, as occasion may require, in order to meet that new situation. This particular Committee was only charged with the duty of considering the law in regard to sedition, and' in regard to seditious propaganda, and it is only in respect to that subject that the report assumes to deal. It is common knowledge, Mr. Speaker, that in Canada to-day there exist many associations and societies developed and organized for the purpose of carrying on a dangerous propaganda, and which, if permitted to pursue their purpose unhindered or unchecked, may ultimately prove a serious menace to our free institutions and to the authority of government in this country. Fortunately, up to the present time, Canada has not suffered to any marked extent from uprisings or from acts of violence or attempted violence which can be directly attributed to these associations, or as a result of their propaganda. In this respect, I think we have been perhaps more favoured than our neighbours in the United States; but we must not permit ourselves to be lulled to rest in any state of fancied security, because it is well known that the same insidious agencies of crime and of revolt which have been operating so freely in the United States, and in some of the countries of Europe, are actually in evidence in Canada to-day-

I think it will be conceded that, these baneful associations in their origin are not native to the soil of this free country; for the most part they are foreign importations, or Canadian imitations of foreign originals. The growth of these societies in this country and in the United States has been very marked in recent times; it is perhaps a development

speechtext:
It may be very difficult under these circumstances to know where the line should be drawn. However, I think the House will agree with me in this-that a line can safely be drawn at that particular point where free speech itself, and where free and unlicensed printing itself, may be in the greatest jeopardy through the dissemination of pernicious doctrine in this country .
With these preliminary remarks, may I be permitted briefly to discuss something of the general scope and application of the amendments proposed by the Committee; and at the outset let me remark that I think it will require rather more than a superficial examination of the various sections of the Criminal Code in order to appreciate the propriety and the significance of some of these recommendations.
The subject of sedition, including seditious language, libels, acts, assemblies and conspiracies, offers a very wide field for legal investigation and research. It will be found that there is a great deal of ancient learning upon the subject. Happily in Canada, that particular branch of our criminal law has up to the present time received very limited application-there has been little or no occasion for it. The cases in this country upon the subject are few and far between; in fact, I think I may say that there is practically no Canadian case law on the subject of sedition. If we seek a definition of this little understood subject, we will have to go to the legal lore of the Motherland. But in England, although we find that the crime of sedition is of very ancient origin, within recent years, indeed, I think I may say for centuries prior to 1914, the law in respect to sedition

has been of exceedingly limited application. I think it may be admitted that both throughout Canada and Great Britain during a long number of peaceful years, there have been many occasions-I might say occasions without number-when language has been used and acts committed, which, according to a strict application or interpretation, of the term "sedition" would have been deemed seditious. Yet the law has been rarely invoked in such cases in times of peace.
Under the free and liberal usages and customs which pertain in Canada and throughout Great Britain such technical breaches of the law have been allowed to pass largely unnoticed. They have been allowed to run their course and to expend their force without let or hindrance on the part of the authorities, and usually with little damage or injury to the community. Indeed, one might say that the policy of passive inaction seems to have been established throughout the British Empire in reigard to sedition in times of peace. The law was certainly not dead, it was on the statute book but it was permitted to remain dormant. Prosecutions were not instituted for every trivial word or act which, upon a strict interpretation, could be called seditious. The ravings of soap box orators upon the street comers of Canadian cities and the infiamatory oratory of the Hyde Park spellbinders in Great Britain were not the occasions of very many prosecutions. In normal, unwarlike times, the good common sense of the masses appeared a sufficient safeguard of the Throne, of the Constitution, of the institutions of the country, and of the rights and privileges of the people.
But a change has undoubtedly come over the face of the world, a change probably attributable in great measure to the war which has recently been brought to a close. The great war has undoubtedly been the author of many changes in the social and political fabric of the world. Many new schools of thought have been established, many new ideals 'of government have been set up, many former idols have been overthrown only to expose feet of clay. The serenity and tranquility of the former era has been succeeded by a period of unrest which is experienced all over the world- unrest accompanied by submerged excitement and by a good deal of uncertainty as to the future. Canada, in common with the other nations of the world, must be prepared resolutely to face the situation, as it exists in this country, and to provide
laws which will reasonably meet that situation.
In the first place we must all fully realize that there is being carried on in Canada at this moment, an organized, concerted, and sustained effort to spread false and pernicious doctrines, designed in the first instance to cause dissatisfaction amongst His Majesty's subjects, to set class against class, to hamper, injure or destroy the public service and designed in their ultimate end, to subvert constituted authority and to overturn government itself. I do not think I have overdrawn the picture of the situation as its exists in Canada to-day.
So far as is known, this propaganda is chiefly carried on by means of associations or societies which have come into existence in great numbers and during very recent times in this country. As a result, of the efforts and operations of these societies Canada is being literally deluged at this moment with literature which one would not hesitate to stamp as seditious even under the provisions of the present law and having regard to the definition of the word "sedition" which I shall give to the House in a moment.
During the active progress of the war, as the House is aware, a fairly strong censorship was maintained under the authority of certain Orders in Council, but since the signing of the armistice that censorship has been very materially relaxed. Likewise, during the war, there have been enactments in force in respect to sedition in its various aspects. These enactments were supplementary to the provisions of the Criminal Code and were embodied in Orders in Council passed under the War Measures Act. Since the armistice was signed these Orders in Council have been rescinded. It has come to the knowledge of the Government, and it came also to the knowledge of the Special Committee through channels which, while absolutely reliable, are more or less confidential, that since the decision of the Orders in Council in regard to sedition, and since the relaxation of the press censorship, which I have just mentioned, there has been a noticeable increase on the one hand in the efforts of certain doubtful associations and societies, and, on the other hand, a large increase in the circulation of seditious literature. The operators are apparently becoming bolder in their operations day by day. It is believed that a considerable portion of this literature is printed, as well as circulated in this country. Perhaps the largest portion of it finds its way into Canada from the United States, through the mails, through express

companies, by freight, by motor truck and otherwise.
I do. not know that any useful purpose would be served if I were to exhibit to the House or place upon Hansard samples of this thoroughly pernicious and seditious literature, nor would it serve any useful purpose to enumerate those doubtful or baneful societies. However, this information may be obtained by any hon. gentleman who desires to afford himself an opportunity of examining it.
It has frequently been said that government by Order in Council is not popular, and that consequently such government is not usually effective. We in Canada are in this position to-day: The Orders in Council which were in force in regard to sedition have been rescinded; the old enactments of our Criminal Code still stand intact. I believe that the time has come when action should be taken by this Parliament to put in statutory form some, at least, of the provisions which did appear in those Orders in Council.
The report does not suggest any radical amendment to the present sections of the Criminal 'Code. Those sections are left intact, with the exception of two slight amendments, to which I will refer in a moment. I might also point out that the new sections proposed by the committee by way of additional provisions and not in substitution of any present enactment. In other words, the proposed amendments are not for the purpose of altering the present law, but of adding to it. An effort has also been made by the committee to have something like uniformity in '[DOT]egard to the various classes of seditious offences so far as the penalty prescribed is concerned.
The committee, I think, fully appreciated and realized the difficulties which beset it. They have made an honest and an earnest effort to bring to the House a reasonable recommendation for amendments which I think are highly necessary to the criminal law at the present time. However, the committee does not feel that it by any means exhausted the subject. In the opinion of the House we may have gone too far, or we may have fallen far short of what we should have done. The committee is quite willing to place itself and its report in the judgment of the House, and if the report can usefully be amended the committee will be only too happy to see it so amended.
The first recommendation which the committee makes is in regard to unlawful associations. There is to-day no provision in our criminal law in that regard. It seems
fMr. Guthrie.]	.
rather odd that there should be none. There is a_ provision known to every lawyer-section 87-which deals with unlawful assemblies. That section provides that an assembly of three or more persons shall become an unlawful assembly if it is so conducted as to give reasonable fear that a ' -each of the peace tumultuously is immi-ent. If the conduct of that assembly become such that anybody reasonably fears a breach of the peace, the assembly becomes unlawful. And once a breach of the peace takes place, the assembly becomes a riot under section 88 of the 'Code. That is the only provision of our law, so far as I have been able to find out, which renders a meeting unlawful.
The proposal of the committee goes much further than anything in the Code to-day. The committee proposes to make unlawful any society or association, incorporated or unincorporated, one of whose purposes, or professed purposes, is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada by use of force, violence, physical injury to person or property, or the like. If these be the purposes, or any of the purposes, of the association or society, it would become under this section an unlawful society, its officers and members under the following subsections will become liable to prosecution and to very serious penalties, and the goods and property of the society will become liable to seizure, forfeiture and confiscation. It will be seen that the proposal of the committee goes very much further than the present law in regard to unlawful assemblies.
Section 2 of the report deals with the present law as contained in our Criminal Code in regard to sedition and seditious offences. I think there is no offence or crime which is so little understood in this country as that of sedition. I doubt if outside of the members of the legal profession any hon. member has a very accurate conception of what the term "sedition" signifies or covers. Up till perhaps a month or so ago I did not have a very accurate idea of it myself. I doubt very much if many lawyers in Canada have any very accurate knowledge of the full meaning and significance of the term, unless they have had occasion to examine into the law. I have taken occasion recently to ask a number of laymen of undoubted general intelligence what their idea was of the term " sedition," and in nearly every instance they have replied that it was treason, that it meant the destruction of the King or other members

of the Royal family-instigation to rebellion or civil war, or something like that.
The popular idea of sedition is that it is something in the nature of treason; but that is entirely erroneous. One difficulty which I think exists to-day in our Criminal Code is that there is no definition of sedition. Consequently we are thrown back upon the common law of England. And when some of the greatest lawyers in England undertook forty years ago to frame a definition of sedition, they reported to the House of Commons the difficulties which they had in framing any accurate definition. In our Criminal Code we have this provision at the present time in section 132, subsection (1) ;
Seditious words are words expressive of a seditious intention.
That does not take us very far.
Subsection (2) : A seditious libel is a libel expressive of a seditious intention.
Subsection (3) : A seditious conspiracy is an agreement between .two or more persons to carry into execution a seditious intention.
I am satisfied that the vast majority of our people do not know what sedition is, and I doubt very much if when speaking or acting or writing they have any knowledge, in many cases, that they are actually transgressing the law.
In 1880 an attempt was made to codify the criminal law of Great Britain. A Royal Commission of very eminent lawyers was appointed for the purpose and a draft Bill was reported to the House of Commons, but that Bill never became law. However, that Royal Commission did attempt to frame a comprehensive definition of the term " sedition," and their definition-which is rather a definition of the term " seditious intention"-is as follows:
" an intention-
(1)	to bring into hatred or contempt or to excite disaffection against the person of Her Majesty, or the government and constitution of the United1 Kingdom or of any part of it as by law established, or either House of Parliament, or the administration of Justice; or
(2)	to excite Her Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, otherwise than by lawful means, the alteration of any matter in church or state by law established ; or
(3)	to raise discontent or disaffection amongst Her Majesty's subjects; or
(4)	to promote feelings of ill-will and hostility between different classes of such subjects."
The Royal Commission reported that the definition which I have just given was as accurate a statement of the existing law as they could frame.
When our Criminal Code was before Parliament in 1892 the original Bill contained that definition. But the Special Committee of the House which dealt with the Bill thought it better to strike out the definition and allow the simple term " sedition " to be put in the section so that the word would carry its full common law significance. The section has stood from 1892 until the present time, just as originally framed. In my humble opinion, it would have far more force, effect and usefulness if the definition had been as it was in the English draft code; people would then have had some reasonable idea of what sedition really consisted. The committee propose to leave that section as it is; anything that has been the law since 1892 in respect of sedition will continue the law.
According to the recommendation of the committee, section 133 is to be struck out. Section 132 makes provision with regard to seditious words or words expressive of a seditious intention. Section 133 is a saving clause, which, in substance provides that if the words are uttered bona fide or in good faith, and for the purpose of remedying some apparent grievance or difficulty, then no offence of sedition shall have been committed. In my opinion, the language of the saving clause is too broad; in practice, it has operated as a cloak or shield which has prevented the imposition of penalties upon offenders who are able to point out to the magistrate or judge that any language they used or words they wrote were written or spoken in good faith for the purpose of pointing out some injustice that ought to be remedied, and that consequently, they were not guilty of sedition. In many cases prosecutions have failed on account of that particular section. My objection to the section is this: That if all a man merely advocates is a lawful change in conditions by the employment of lawful means, that is not a seditious offence. If he acts bona fide and advocates only lawful means, it cannot be seditious; the act becomes seditious only when the man advocates the employment of unlawful means to accomplish a purpose or to achieve an end. Consequently, I do not see very much use for section 133; and it is evident from information which came to the committee that recently, under this section, a number of prosecutions have failed in certain parts of the country.
In regard to section 134, which is the penal clause, the committee has recommended that the penalty be struck out. At



present the penalty is only two years; we have asked that the penalty be made from one to twenty years, which is the penalty we have recommended in respect of the other seditious offences as set out in our report.
The next clause of the report deals with a very important subject, namely, that of printing and circulating seditious literature. It may be argued that under section 133 of the Code as it is to-day a prosecution for seditious libel may take place. That is very true, and if a new clause, as drafted by the committee, is placed in the Code, a prosecution for seditious libel may still take place under section 133 or under the new section 97B. The difference between the two is this: in the section which the committee has recommended | we have endeavoured clearly to set out what is a seditious publication. The section reads:
"97B. Any person who prints, publishes, edits, issues, circulates, sells, offers for sale or distiibution -any book, n -wspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture paper, circular, card, letter, writing, print, publication or document of any kind, in which is taught, advocated, advised o-r defended, or who shall in any manner teach, advocate, advise, or defend the use, without authority of law, of force, violence, terrorism, or -physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, as a means of accomplishing any governmental, industrial or economic change, or otherwise, shall he guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for not less than one year, and not more than twenty years.
If the Committee's recommendation is carried out, in the future a prosecution may take place either under that new section or under section 133 of the Code as it now stands, or under both sections.
But we have gone a little further. We have made it a criminal offence to attempt to circulate or to circulate through the mails of this country any such literature -as is described in the section which I have just read. At present there is no adequate provision in our law to prevent the circulation of seditious literature through the post office. There is a clause in the Post Office Act, section 9, which permits the Postmaster General to make regulations in regard to certain matters

to provide that no dangerous, contraband or other improper articles shall be placed therein, and also to formd the use of the mails for the forwarding of any article tne importation of which is prohibited by law, but no penalties are prescribed. We have recommended a rather drastic section in regard to the use of Canadian mails for the circulation of seditious literature. In the opinion of the Committee, the section of the Post Office Act to which

I have referred was not sufficient, and it is now provided that any person who uses the mails for this purpose and is convicted thereof shall be liable to a penalty of from one to twenty years' imprisonment.
The next clause is a provision against the importation into Canada of seditious literature. As I have stated, We have absolute evidence that a fairly large portion of the seditious literature now in circulation is actually printed in Canada; but there is no doubt that a large portion is imported from the United States. There are provisions in our Customs Act, sections 15 and 17 and schedule C, which together provide against the importation into Canada of any seditious literature, but no penalty is by that Act attached to the offence.
The only power of the Customs Department in respect to such importation would be to seize and destroy it, and the man who imported it into Canada is not liable upon any criminal charge. The section which the committee recommends would make it a criminal offence and subject any one guilty of an infringment of the law to a penalty of from one year to twenty years' imprisonment.
Then there is a general provision which makes it the duty of every employee of the Post Office Department or other departments of the Government of Canada to seize any seditious literature wheresoever it may be found, whether in the mails, or in or upon stations, wharves, yards, cars, trucks, motors or other vehicles, or steamboats, and there is a further provision that the literature when seized shall be confiscated and destroyed.	.
Sir SAM HUGhES: Is the party to whom the literature is addressed, supposing it comes through the mails, the guilty one or will it be the one sending it?

subsubtopic: SPEECH OF SOLICITOR GENERAL MOVING ADOPTION OF REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The party to whom it is addressed cannot be guilty under this clause. It was suggested that the clause should go a little further and that we should make it a criminal offence to have in one's possession any seditious literature. One of the Orders in Council which were passed during the period of the war made the possession of seditious literature a criminal offence. You would, however, subject many innocent people to prosecution if a provision of that kind were included in the Act. A man cannot control the situation for himself. Evilly disposed people may mail seditious literature to you, and it will reach you through the post office. Other persons may systematically

distribute it at house doors, and it gets into the household, and it would be rather a radical enactment to say that a man was guilty of a serious offence in this country merely by reason of the fact that seditious literature was found in his possession. If the House is of opinion that the clause should be extended in that way, a few words will do that. We could insert in the second line of clause 97 B these words:
" Or who has in his possession without lawful excuse."
But in the opinion of the committee that provision was a little more drastic than the occasion required.
These are, briefly stated, the recommendations of the Special Committee. It may by some be thought that they are rather radical and that the penalties imposed are higher than the occasion requires. I can only point out that the Congress of the United States has imposed much higher penalties. It is within the knowledge of us all that in certain prosecutions for sedition which took place in the United States last summer, Judge Landis of Chicago imposed prison terms of thirty years, and last week a Bill was introduced at Washington to provide the death penalty in cases where bombs or explosives are sent through the mails, and to provide the death penalty upon any one who belongs to an anarchist society. The penalties imposed in the United States "within the last year or a year and a half are much higher than anything the committee has proposed in this report. The situation is grave, both in Canada and in the United States. Whether much will be accomplished by changes in the Criminal law in lessening the gravity of the situation, it is hard to say, but I believe it to be the duty of this Parliament to make ample and adequate provision for the situation which undoubtedly exists in Canada to-day. I, therefore, move:
That the report of the Special Committee appointed to consider and report on laws relating to sedition and seditious propaganda he concurred in.

subsubtopic: SPEECH OF SOLICITOR GENERAL MOVING ADOPTION OF REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if this motion be debatable now I should like, without any desire at all to interfere with the regular order of business expected to be proceeded with this afternoop, to say a word or two with reference to the report of the Special Committee and the observations of the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie). Judging by the manner in which the House received the hon. gentleman's reference to the subject of free speech and the rights of organized labour, I take
209J
it that there is, at the present time, in any event, a unanimous opinion in this House that free speech and the rights of organized labour should not be interfered with. However that may be, such was the opinion that prevailed in the committee of which I was a member, and the report from which-not from the whole of which, however-is now before the House. There was in the committee a very sharp division of opinion as to the necessity of amending the Criminal Code, and there was a further division of opinion whether, in the event of the committee being of opinion that the Criminal Code with reference to sedition and seditious propaganda should be amended-in view of the numerous strikes and the general unrest throughout the country-this was the proper time to make such a report to the House and to induce a discussion of matters that would inevitably be discussed by reason of that report and of any action that might follow the introduction of that report. It was on the latter ground principally-coupled with the fact that an opinion prevailed that the present Criminal Code was ample to cover the class of cases to which the attention of the committee was directed-that a portion of the committee, including myself, shared the view that this was not the proper time to introduce such a report as that, the adoption of which has now been moved by the Solicitor General. He himself, in his interesting historical and legal address, showed that that view on the part of a portion of the committee was well founded, because he informed the -House that just as soon as the report was introduced, a newspaper, the name of which I do not know, published an article to the effect that this report would have a bearing upon the strike and the rights of labour organizations engaged in the strike at Winnipeg. Such was not the intention of, but such was the fear entertained by a number of members of the Committee. That fact explains why on the day of the last sitting of the Committee there was at one stage of that sitting a majority of the members of the Committee then present opposed to the bringing in of a report at this particular time. As to the determination to maintain law and order in this country and to enforce respect and obedience for law and order, there never was any question amongst the members of the Committee, but the opportune ness of action at this particular time was a subject upon which there was a sharp difference of opinion, and it seems to me that the very incident referred to by the Solid-

tor General shows that those who held that opinion had good ground for holding it.
My hon. friend has referred to the fact that in his judgment there is necessity for some such drastic amendments as are proposed by the report, because the Orders in Council dealing with sedition have been rescinded. I have only to observe on that phase, that according to the information given to the Committee, the offences with respect to sedition and seditious propaganda were committed at a time when those Orders in Council were in force, and in my opinion action should have been taken then, and the delay until this Committee sat, deliberated, and a portion of it concurred in the bringing in of this report, should not have occurred.
The time for action with regard to the practices with reference to which the committee was informed has long since passed, and the question in the minds of a portion of the committee was whether it would not do more harm than good to introduce this subject in the House for discussion at the present time. Because of that view prevailing, there was on the day of the last sitting of the committee a majority of the committee in the room at a certain time actually opposed to the bringing in of the report. The others who remained until the conclusion of the sitting did not submit a minority report, for the reason that they wished to avoid the very discussion which has been evoked here this afternoon, and such further discussion as may take place. Having informed the House of the division of opinion that prevailed in the committee, and as to the points on which that division of opinion existed, I shall reserve anything further I may have to say on the subject until a future occasion, if the report of the committee is concurred in and legislation based upon it is introduced in the House.
Motion agreed to, and report concurred in.

subtopic: VOTES AND PROCEEDINGS AND JOURNALS OF THE HOUSE.
VOTES AND PROCEEDINGS AND JOURNALS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: That the report of the Special Committee appointed to consider the question of consolidating the Votes and Proceedings and Journals of the House of Commons with a view to economy he concurred in.

subtopic: VOTES AND PROCEEDINGS AND JOURNALS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: VOTES AND PROCEEDINGS AND JOURNALS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The House will remembei that some time ago a special committee was appointed to consider the advisability of preparing a report to consolidate what is commonly known as the Votes and Pro-

ceedings, and Journals of the House of Commons. As the House knows, the Votes and Proceedings are what might be termed an informal record of the proceedings of the House, and are distributed from day to day. The Journals are the more formal documents, and at the end of the session are prepared by the proper officer and distributed as a bound volume to the members. The Votes and Proceedings are also distributed as a bound volume. The committee went carefully into the matter and thought the time had arrived when, by a very slight change in phraseology, the Votes and Proceedings and Journals might be incorporated into one document without their being any loss of information to the members of the House. Pursuant to that conclusion, the report of the committee was drawn, recommending that hereafter there be one set only of documents, and that a bound volume be distributed to the members at the end of the session, but that no bound volume taking the place of what is commonly known as the Votes and Proceedings be distributed. It is estimated that this will effect a saving in the neighbourhood of from 810,000 to $12,000 a year. I think that the committee were of the opinion that the House would be equally well served.

subtopic: VOTES AND PROCEEDINGS AND JOURNALS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: I was a member of that committee and concurred in the report, the motion for the reception of which I now second. I must say that at first I was averse to the change contemplated, and when you, Mr. Speaker, consulted me a few weeks before the session opened as to the propriety of this change I informed you that I should like to have the opinion of the then oldest member of the House by many years-the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He knew the ancient usages of Parliament and was very familiar with the rules of this House, and I consulted with him and he afterwards consulted with you, Mr. Speaker, and his opinion was that we could well afford to do away with this one volume because it is practically an exact duplication of the other. I have to correct my hon. friend's statement as to the saving which it was estimated would be affected. From the statement which was placed before us it appeared that the saving would be between $25,000 and $26,000 a year. Under the circumstances I thought that I should follow Sir Wilfrid Laurier's advice, as it would mean a considerable reduction in the expenditure.
Motion agreed to, and report concurred in.
