Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the House this afternoon I feel that a duty is incumbent upon me. This is, in fact, the first session during five years which it was possible for me to attend, and I am confronted with an agreeable task in this particular-the task of voicing my sentiments of gratitude for the sympathy and the interest shown me in the years of my exile and captivity. That duty I have endeavoured to discharge on all occasions that presented themselves to me, whether speaking in public or in private, since the day I set my foot on the blessed shores of Canada.
Exile and captivity are necessarily accompanied in all circumstances by sufferings of a mental, moral, and physical nature; and if I dare in your presence, Mr. Speaker, and in the presence of hon. gentlemen in this House-I, whose lot during the universal catastrophe has not been any more unfavourable than that of many others-to refer to my own personal and painful experiences, I pray you to believe it is not that I intend to single them out. But I feel that no word of mine could more adequately express my gratitude, through you to the Government and to members on both sides of this House, than by saying that during the long years of prison life the repeated manifestations of sympathy on the part of hon. members of this House of Commons have been to me a source of consolation, a source of encouragement, and a source of comfort. I had been regularly kept informed of the efforts made, and of the steps taken, in turn by the Canadian Government and the Imperial authorities to secure my release, both governments being, as I know, supported staunchly and constantly by influences, religious and lay, which, on one fiart for humanitarian reasons and on the other part on personal grounds, had been exercised in my behalf.
To the Canadian Government, to the Imperial Government, and to the influences, beneficent indeed, which have been exercised in my favour, and which have undoubtedly largely contributed, and which certainly aided to a large extent towards my release, and my ultimate exchange, I beg to extend, through you, Mr. Speaker, my deepest gratitude.
When Parliament convened in the month of February, the hon. the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) and the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb), the chief whip of the Liberal party, both gentlemen Obeying the generous sentiments of their hearts, pronounced a few words of praise and of welcome, addressing them to my humble person. The occasion might have been, under ordinary circumstances, propitious for me then to answer, but at that moment Canada was dominated by a deep sorrow and a bitter grief. Her most illustrious son, whose life had been so intimately connected with the history of the country, had been removed from our midst by the inexorable hand of death, and I felt then that any personal reference to me would have been considered an unwelcome distraction from the emotion, and the pious sentiment of sorrow, of pain, and of affection, which penetrated the soul of every citizen of Canada. Had 1 on that occasion chosen to speak I would not have refused to accept

those words that were pronounced and addressed to me by the Acting Prime Minister and by my hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb)-not that I would have thought that I deserved them, but rather because I felt that they were meant for and directed to the tens of thousands-yes, hundreds of thousands-of Canadians, brave men, who had in the course of the last five years left everything behind them-home, and the comforts of home; parents, and all that is tender and cherishable in the home, comforts, friendships-to pass over the deep, that they might uphold on the battlefields of Europe the principles of international faith and justice which were disowned and treated with utter contempt by one of the belligerents.
That those principles of international right and justice have been disowned, I am an eye-witness. It was my privilege, or my misfortune, to be in Belgium at the moment the war broke out. May I in this debate refer just for a moment to that country. Belgium was attacked without provocation. Having been attacked it was invaded. Having been invaded it was conquered, and being conquered it was subjected to infamies political, administrative, and military, which have aroused the universal conscience of the civilized world. It is against the dark background of those infamies that the virtue and the heroism of Belgium shines out in immortal lustre. Two men principally in Belgium embodied the resistance of the nation-one, the- King; the other, Cardinal Mercier.
*Of these two patriots, one at the head of the army, was the soul of the active resistance; the other, within Belgium, in the occupied territory, was the soul of the passive resistance.
But whether we have regard to Belgium as a nation, or whether we have regard to her king, or whether we consider her civil population, or her army, or whether we take all as they constitute one single, noble whole, the picture excites the admiration of the world.
The glory and fame of Canada attaches to the fact that Canada stood by the word of Mr. Asquith, that word uttered in his famous speech at the Guildhall on the 9th of November, 1914, when, speaking in the name of England, Mr. Asquith said: " We have not drawn the sword lightly, and we will not sheathe the sword until Belgium recovers all, and more than all, of that she has sacrificed." Her vindication is complete to-day, right has dethroned might; the principles of moral and public right, which
[Mr. Bfiland, |
form the true basis of nations, have entrenched themselves where it was attempted to enthrone the principles of hegemony and cruel domination.
Many forces have contributed to this achievement; 'Canada has done her share and the men of Canada who participated in the struggle-the forever glorious struggle- are now re-entering their homes. They are welcomed from one end of the country to the other.
But, as they come back, we find they are different from what they were before they left us. During the days of their youth and adolescence they had been taught to develop amongst themselves a spirit of personal initiative. Individualism and particularism had been cultivated among them, but in the years of the war, the energies that were formerly directed towards trade, production, economic development and social welfare were concentrated upon a single aim and under a sole direction in which they had no participation. For four years they have been taught the arts of war, the arts that are destructive and inhuman; now they will have to cultivate the arts of peace, the arts that are constructive and human.
The task that confronts the Government of the country is, indeed, formidable. But, remembering the time when this country absorbed 300,000 immigrants annually, one might very well ask, why should the task be so overvjhelming? We know that the bulk of that immigration was absorbed in this country without any dislocation of the body politic or economic. There are many reasons why the returning soldiers should be looked upon in a different light. Their mentality and aspirations are different. There are also their peculiar requirements to be kept in mind. A few weeks ago in this House the hon. the Minister of Colonization (Mr. Calder) referred to this point in particular, and he said very properly, I think, that it was to be expected that soldiers coming back from Europe should have different views and aspirations from those which they had before the war. It may be incongruous to compare the returned soldier to the immigrant-the immigrant comes to this country knowing that he is a stranger. True, he is invited; true he is induced to come, but he cannot help thinking when he is disembarking that he is entering a country where no special place has been marked out for him. The returned soldier comes back to his home, takes his place by the fireside, and has extended to him a cordial welcome. He knows that his memory has

been kept warm in his mother's heart, in his father's heart, in the hearts of his friends, and the warmth of this feeling finds expression when he comes back- many have been wounded, perhaps crippled. Were the conditions prevailing in Canada at the present time the conditions that prevailed before the war, the problem which confronts the people of this country, and in particular the Government which has the authority to deal with it, would be singularly simplified. The war has left upon Canada its mark as it has left its mark elsewhere. It is true that we have been spared the destruction of property and the devastation which has befallen many of the countries of Europe, particularly France and Belgium. But Canada has -felt the war very sorely. Industries have been, to a certain degree, dislocated; activities of all kinds have been- adapted to the necessities of the hour; woman has found employment in some fields which previously invited only the industry of men. Moreover, a great financial burden is bearing down upon- the shoulders of the people.
Faced with these conditions, I ask myself, and I ask the House: What policy would be best calculated to remedy the curse of un-employmenit? In some provinces, and notably in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan- and Alberta, there are still millions of acres of fertile land which await only the sturdy hand of the tiller. As to the fertility and productiveness of the land we can entertain no doubt if we are to rely on the numberless reports that are at our disposal.	-
In no epoch of history before this has agriculture revealed itself as of more paramount importance. Agriculture is the mother industry, it is at the very foundation of the needs of life itself. Other industries may live, but should it become necessary to select on industry only, that one would be agriculture. The tiller of the soil is king, his realm is nature, her luxuriant beauty is his, his horizon is boundless, the atmosphere he breathes is pure and recuperating. He is unconcerned about the hundred and one niceties and subtleties which surround the beehives of industry, for he serves one master only, the One above, and he caters to our own mother earth, who treats him as her most beloved child.
I would that we had hundreds of Dr. Robertsons, who at the head of a regiment would invade our virgin lands that are fit for cultivation. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that in those new and peaceful fields they would accomplish a task no less glorious than that they accomplished in war, and for which a concert of praise ascends from the lips of every true patriot.
Though the captains of agriculture are not as numerous as we would wish, is it to be contended that we should renounce the establishment of our returned soldiers on the land? I say no. The Government has extended to the returned soldier some inducements in the way of cash assistance. The bona fide settler now is, if I judge aright, perhaps in a position to receive as much as $8,000 by way of loan. On both sides of the House I am sure we will consider this move to be commendable. But it is not sufficient. The incentive should be larger; it should not be limited to this loan in money.
And what other inducement can you extend to the farmer? Give him a fiscal policy which will invite him to the land and which will help him to create wealth for the country. Men on the farm have a special claim to our attention, because primarily this is an agricultural country.
That brings me forcibly to a consideration of the fiscal policy which this country should adopt. During the eighteen years that I have had a seat in this House our fiscal -policy has been the bone of contention as between free traders on the one side and protectionists on the other. The manufacturing interests and the farming interests have been at loggerheads. The farmer is in Canada to stay, and the manufacturer also is in Canada to stay. Their interests, one is forced to recognize, are in some degree divergent, and whilst I am not prepared to embrace the cause of the one to the entire exclusion of the cause of the other, I am inclined to think that the . manufacturer has had the advantage from the different Governments of this country. He was better organized, he was better supported financially for propaganda work, and especially in the period of his early youth and development a full measure of assistance in the shape of a protective tariff was extended to him.
The manufacturer has accomplished great things for Canada-and, perhaps I may add, for himself also. It would be an insult to his -spirit of manhood to contend that he still needs to the -same degree the assistance which was so generously granted ito him by the farmer and the consumer in the days of his youth. I do not want to offend the manufacturer by supposing for one moment that he is not able to compete with his foreign competitor, when in many instances he has held his own remarkably

well in the markets of the world. I do not need any other' demonstration of that than the fact that in this House a few weeks ago the member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie)-an avowed protectionist himself- declared that in his own industry he had secured a pronounced success in the markets of other lands.
We are told that this is an era of reconstruction and readjustment. The main feature of this reconstruction is admittedly the civil re-establishment of the returned soldiers, and a pressing invitation is conveyed to our brave boys to enter the field of agriculture. I say to the Government: Extend to them all possible assistance in that direction, especially in the shape of a tariff that will relieve their shoulders from the heavy burden of taxation that is now bearing down upon them.
It is generally contended that the farmer is the most prosperous of our citizens. I myself am in a position to judge quite accurately the condition of the farmer, for I come from a farming constituency, and I am descended from a farming family. I have no hesitation in corroborating the statement that was made at Belleville, Ont., last January by no less a light in the agricultural world than Professor A. Leitch. Speaking there, after an investigation on a number of farms in the county of Oxford, Ont., this eminent professor was of the opinion that the farmer was barely making a living. He said in particular-and this will be a very short quotation:-
It is next to impossible, unless a man has an enormously large farm, to make over $2,000 a year, and that only by working thirteen hours a day.
Professor Leitch continues to say that the results are not due to bad management, because some of the most efficient men, the best animals, and the highest crop yields were to be found on these farms, but in most of the cases that were brought under his observation on farms of about 45 acres, with about 40 acres of tillable land and 32 acres of actual crop, the owners only averaged $524 of labour income, representing the salary of the farmer and of his wife and children.
The farmer wants free agricultural implements; he wants the free admission into Canada of articles which are necessary in the furnishing of a home. The farmer wants these concessions, because he needs them-
I say to the Government: Grant them to him.
As the years go by it is apparent to me that Canada should have ratified the reciprocal trade agreement with United States

in 1911. The fact that a large portion of the community refused to endorse the scheme is not, in my estimation, an indication that the country was against it. A keen observer of the political events of that day will admit with me the reciprocity proposal was refused for other reasons than economic reasons. Moreover, during the few months that I have been back in this country I have noticed, as you, Mr. Speaker, and members of the House have no doubt noticed, that resolutions have been adopted generally by farming communities asking for the enforcement of the Fielding trade agreement. Can we ignore the request of what I sincerely believe to be the majority of the Canadian people?
Did the Fielding reciprocity agreement provide for free agricultural implements?

A very substantial reduction was provided for in the reciprocity proposals submitted to Parliament under the Laurier Administration.
I can hear the strong protests of the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie); I can hear their words of warning-perhaps I should say their words of threatening. Should this Government go one step further in lowering the walls which constitute an almost insuperable obstacle to the entry of foreign goods into Canada, then, according to their view the whole industrial fabric of Canada would be washed away as a chip on the sand by the wave of low-priced imports.
And then, the argument of the adverse balance of trade is invoked. I shall not busy myself even for a moment with these exponents of the argument concerning balance of trade. I shall content myself with saying that trade, well-understood trade, rests upon the interchange of goods. Endeavour to flood the market of the foreigner, succeed, if that is possible, in excluding the foreigner from your market, and the process will lead to abnormal charges, to abnormal rates of exchange; and, if the two countries are of about the same population, to the impoverishment of the country you are exploiting, the inevitable result will be the destruction of the customer whom you prized so much and whom you were exploiting so merrily. Yes, trade, in order to be profitable and enduring, must be reciprocal.
The Government, by its new proposals, has taken steps to secure new markets. I was not aware that Canada needed markets at the present time; what she needs ' especially is commodities-the products of

the farm and the products of manufacture. But be that as it may, the Government has taken steps to advance credits to some nations-to Roumania, to Greece, to Belgium, to France, and, if I am correctly informed, to Italy also. I believe that much could be gained from the markets of France and Belgium, especially during their period of reconstruction. But Roumania and Greece are in too close proximity to countries where social and political conditions are still unsettled and in doubt, and I would urge the Government to be very cautious about extending credits too large to those countries.
But we have markets; there is the market to the south of us, and we have the market of England. Although our goods are admitted free to England, ^.he United States is still the country with which we have the largest trade. That shows that you cannot combat the laws of geography and the laws of nature. Perhaps some hon. gentlemen will be surprised when I say that before the war Canada supplied to England only one-fifth of its import of wheat. In the line of leather and leather goods, our trade with England was pitiably low; in fruit and in cattle it was not what it should have been; in the line of lumber, of pulp and of paper, products which are very closely allied, the market of England should open an almost boundless field for our exporters. The products of the fisheries should have a good place in the market of England. It would be an error to develop this country too much on the side of manufacture and not enough on the side of agriculture. But let me refer to one or two lines of manufactured products so far as our export to England is concerned. England in 1913 imported $40,000,000 worth of carriages, and out of that amount Canada supplied almost nothing. The same may be said of England's imports of shoes.
It is hinted in the newspapers that England should enter on a policy of Imperial preference. If she should do so, the produce of Canada would enjoy a protection or preference on the English market. Let us then develop our trade, especially with the natural resources of this country.
As regards the subject of immigration, what should be the course to adopt. Whatever proportion of returned soldiers may conceivably be placed upon farms, a large number will have to be absorbed by industry. Unemployed men are walking the streets of our cities by tens of thousands. Should this army of idle men be increased? I say: No. I say: Stop immigration for a
while at least. I am ready to concede that an increase in population is conducive to prosperity, as is demonstrated by the example of the United States in the last century and by the example of Canada since 1896; but at the present moment I believe our immigration should be confined to farm labourers and domestic servants of irreproachable physical and moral soundness. It is very doubtful whether unrestricted inmigration at this time would not increase our present unfavourable social and economic conditions.
One guarantee of the early restoration of normal conditions in Canada is the conviction that must prevail in all sections that, during the years of heroism and stress through which the country has just passed, Canada's autonomy as a nation in the great British Empire has been preserved in its integrity. Can we boast-can the Government boast of having preserved our complete autonomy during the war? I am afraid that under the spell and influence of the war, the representatives of Canada in the councils of the British Empire have allowed unsound advice to prevail with them. They have listened too complacently to extraneous influences; and mark you, Sir, in making these remarks, I am making them in the interest of the British Empire itself. Statesmen whose political inheritance is highly prized: Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Thompson, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, have reiterated the theme that complete autonomy exercised without undue pressure or influence is the greatest safeguard for the permanency and solidity of the British Empire.
il deeply regret in this connection the Siberian expedition. Am I alone in this House in regretting it? Am I alone in the country in looking upon it with dismay? No, the number of those who disagree with the Government is, perhaps, greater than is thought. After eight months of sojourn in Canada, I have yet to meet a man who approves this scheme, much less one who is enthusiastic over it. Whether the expedition to Siberia should have been undertaken at all is a debatable question, which might well be answered in the negative. But granted, if you like, that the Siberian expedition should have been embarked upon, by what process of reasoning should Canada, after a contribution of 400,000 men to the Allied armies of Europe, be called upon to supply a share, especially when we know that one of our allies, and not one of the least, Japan, one

of the Big Five, has not contributed any more than a few thousand men, and that those few thousand men from Japan were used to wrest from Germany, Tsing-Tau, the only foothold, the only fortress that Germany had in the Far East. One may refer to the part played by Japan in Mediterranean waters against the submarine menace, and I am ready to concede that Japan has done something in the Mediterranean sea. I do not want to minimize her effort; but apart from that, it must be admitted that Japan has been absent from all theatres of war. A situation which is considered serious develops in eastern Russia, in the immediate neighbourhood of Nippon island. Japan has an available army of
3,000,000 men, well equipped, well trained and well disciplined, one-quarter of which would be sufficient to remedy any situation that was considered deficient in eastern Russia. Japan, moreover, is within a few hours of the new theatre of war. But we are confronted with the bare, cold and shocking fact that Canadian troops, after a contribution of men unexampled in this country, after the sacrifice of 50,000 lives, after casualties that have reached a total of over 100,000, after an outlay in money of about $1,000,000,000, are despatched to the Antipodes to fight whom? Nobody knows. This expedition was a political error, a military mistake, and a wanton extravagance. Are the people of Canada responsible? Is Parliament responsible? The people of Canada and Parliament were not consulted. Who, then, is responsible? The Government is responsible. A few weeks ago, when this subject was broached in Parliament, the President of Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) and the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Mewburn), in their eagerness to exonerate the Government, answered that the expedition to Siberia had been asked for by the Imperial Government. Either the representatives of Canada in the War Cabinet have agreed to this or they have dissented from it. If they have approved the scheme, then they have shown a disposition to yield that is lamentable and that will be so considered by the country at large. If they opposed the idea their opposition was disregarded; they were outvoted. If that be the case, I ask: What becomes of Canadian autonomy? During my stay in London last year it was represented to me that a body of men, some Canadians and some English, not members of this Government, were the power behind the Throne, the inspiring mmu behind tins scheme.

If it succeeded, it would be perhaps a decisive move, and the principle of the shaping of Canadian policy in London, If not resented and condemned in Canada, would have been accepted and consecrated. It is of the utmost importance in the reestablishment of normal conditions in Canada that our people should not be under the impression that a body of men whose motives and interests are foreign, if not adverse, to true Imperial and Canadian interests, have a commanding "voice in the shaping of Canadian policy. On the score of autonomy, as on the score of the franchise, the Canadian people are sensitive. Both prerogatives are of the highest political order, and interference with either must lead to dissatisfaction and unrest. With a full sense of my responsibility as a member of this Parliament I say to my hon. friends: preserve both the one and the other. Autonomy for the nation, and the franchise for the individual, are the twin pillars upon which rests the magnificent structure of a free Canada in a free British Empire.
The declarations which have been made so far in connection with the new Franchise Bill are of a very vague character, so much so that it is impossible for any one outside of those engaged upon its preparation to foresee what its main features will be. Since my return I have found in Canada the opinion prevalent among many classes that the War-time Elections Act has accomplished very little for the country, while, it has caused any amount of discontent and dissatisfaction. Indeed, in unpopularity, it ranks next to the Siberian Expedition. But I shall refrain from discussing the merits or the demerits of the Act which is now the law of the land; I may not have been able to grasp the situation that existed at the time of its adoption; but whether necessary or unnecessary the law is certainly unfortunate. By it thousands.of citizens have been deprived of the most precious privilege of a British citizen-the franchise. In every British country the franchise is the corner-stone of all liberty, and let not the House construe my advocacy of a generous franchise as advocating that the full privileges of citizenship should be granted to men who are not in perfect accord and sympathy with our established institutions and our ethics of nationhood. Nothing could be more remote from my mind. But we want to make it clear that this is a country with democratic tendencies, as opposed to the accursed and now obsolete system of rule

by the few. Let me repeat here what I have said elsewhere, that a franchise law in the hands of a government may be as dangerous a weapon as a sword in the hands of the despot. Not one, I hope, wishes to ' disfranchise men simply because they do not share their views as to the policy that should be adopted for promoting the advancement of the nation, moral, economic, and social.
That is their only reason.

In this Parliament there are now five or six vacant seats. Why should not those constituencies be represented? In the early part of the session the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) introduced a Bill providing for the holding of a by-election automatically in case of a vacancy occurring. The rules of the House preclude my hon. friend from pressing his Bill to a conclusion at this stage of the session, but I appeal to the Government to take it up and make it a government measure. I can assure them that it would pass this House and become the law of the land within fifteen minutes. Then when a vacancy occurred by reason of the death or resignation of the sitting member the people of that constituency would be called upon within sixty days to elect a new representative. We are very prone to take our examples from Great Britain-in England a by-election automatically takes place within six or seven weeks of a vacancy occurring.
The conviction is widespread that this horrible war with its cortege of suffering and bereavement has been accepted and fought by the allied nations for the safeguarding of liberty-of liberty threatened by a despotic power-and the hope has penetrated all our souls that out of the terrible chaos of the last four years something may emerge better than what the world had hitherto known. A sad hour indeed it would be for the people of this country, and of all countries, if they should realize that freedom of thought,
5 p.m. freedom of speech, freedom of the press, and freedom of the franchise, have been curtailed instead of enlarged as a result of the severe ordeal which has been undergone. There are those who think, or profess to think, that government without the concurrence of the people or of Parliament is to be preferred. On the other hand, there are those who contend with Abraham Lincoln for government of the people, by the people, and for the people.
In Belgium in 1915, during eight months of the German occupation, and later in Germany, I was in close contact with the protagonists of the first-mentioned theory, with the disciples of him who believed that rule by the few was preferable. When I left this country I think I was a democrat, but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that now after having come in contact with the men who shared the view that rule by the few is preferable, I have decided to remain unalterably attached to the largest possible measure of popular liberty. At the present moment, when clouds which are slow to dissipate overhang all nations, when in some instances established institutions have been overthrown, when unrest and disquietude is felt in some quarters, it is of paramount importance, both with regard to the franchise and to autonomy that the Government, like Caesar's wife, should be above suspicion.
1 had intended, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words on the financial situation, but I will not dwell at any length upon this subject which was treated in so masterly a manner by my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. Mac-Master) yesterday. I cannot refrain from admitting that the Minister of Finance displayed a good deal of frankness in presenting his Budget proposals. He depicted the financial situation of Canada as indeed not very rosy and as being rather gloomy; but, Sir, I believe there is no room in this country for pessimism. The burden is serious, but it can be carried. The debt of Canada being $2,000,000,000, and the nation within a few months having to pay $40,000,000 for pensions; the annual outlay on these obligations will reach a total of $155,000,000. This is a very large sum indeed, and yet after we have met it we shall not yet have spent a single dollar to carry on the affairs of the country. The sum of $155,000,00 is about double what the whole revenue of Canada was twenty years ago. The national debt will be $2,000,000,000 next year. What will it be the year after next? And what will it be after even another year has expired? I venture to say that within three years it will reach the figure of $2,500,000,-
000.	There is a saving feature about it: we owe the money to our own people. The _ Minister of Finance laid a good deal of stress on this point, indeed he contended that it was very much more advantageous that we should owe the money to the Canadian people. It is true that when you come to pay the interest on the public debt you pay it to your own people; but we must not overlook the fact that although the

money was spent in Canada it was money out of the pockets of the people and not money brought into the Dominion from a foreign country. Therefore, while in one respect that fact is advantageous, in the other it is not. Production and economy is the motto preached by the Minister of Finance. I admit that we must produce; it is the only manner in which the affairs of the country can be carried on to a successful end. At this moment, when a large portion of Europe is devastated, when the people there are clamouring for commodities of all kinds, the duty of the Government should be to tap the-natural resources of Canada to the uttermost; and these words of Mr. Auckland Geddes, pronounced at the Imperial Chamber of Commerce a few days ago, have their full application here:
Trade on a huge and hitherto unexampled scale is the only way by which we can make good the losses of the war.
We must practise economy. That was the predication of the Minister of Finance. I am afraid the advice will be futile because the Government of which the hon. gentleman is a member has not supported the predication by example. Large amounts of money have been expended. The cost of registration, to which reference was made yesterday, to the country, has been $650,000. The Minister of Public Works said the brakes must be applied and applied very soon, but it is not for us to do that,-the responsibility rests upon the Government. We have been voting moneys during the present session, (and I notice the same thing occurred in the previous session,) for works that are not productive of revenue, and that are not advantageous to the country. They create, perhaps, an ephemeral inflated prosperity, but that will only lead in a few years to further unrest.
Although the Minister of Finance has not intimated it very plainly, a loan pf a very respectable size will be launched in Canada before long, a loan probably of $300,000,000. Next year, with a deficit in sight of some $320,000,000 or $340,000,000, another loan will be launched, and then perhaps the year .following, a third loan. I want to impress upon the Government the importance of not exempting these loans from income tax, because if that is done the taxation will have to be imposed on consumption and then the poor, the masses of the people, that are less able to carry the burden, will be overladen, which in due course will lead to further unrest and dissatisfaction.

The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion)) last night in a very able speech, which I followed with the greatest pleasure, referred to the existing labour unrest in this country. In that hon. gentleman's estimation there are several causes for the industrial trouble. In my estimation, Mr. Speaker, these are the causes of labour unrest: First, the conviction, properly arrived at, that the war was carried to a successful end by the masses, second, a keener realization on the part of the masses of the people of the shocking inequalities of the social world, and third, a common suffering everywhere, because of the high cost of living. What is the remedy? It is to try to afford a better standard of life to the labouring community, and to reduce the cost of living. Reduce the cost of living, is a fine phrase, but how are you going to do it? It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that you can reduce the cost of living by applying yourself to the three following activities: Increasei production, reduce the taxation on consumption, and in particular bring the profiteer to account. The two former methods I have already referred to during my remarks; but whatever may be the amount of production, be it ample or small, the cost to the consumer may not be diminished by reason of an immoral disposition on the part of some human beings to take undue advantage of a faulty system of distribution. There exists the law of supply and demand. If that law is allowed to have freedom, if it is allowed to follow its natural course, it will operate according to reason and will prevent the oppression of the masses.
But, the just and free operation of the law of supply and demand has been ignored or rather interfered with. Contact has been lost between the original producer and the ultimate consumer. Between the two a parasite or tremendous dominating power has entrenched himself. He is to be found in the warehouse, in the cold storage plant, where he accumulates and holds for a rise in price and a scandalous profit. You would have found him between the consumer and the producer seven or eight weeks ago when the price -of butter was sent up to seventy-five cents a pound. Had not spring threatened him, the price might have been carried to $1 a pound. Have we not in this country an Act known as the War Measures Act which gives to the Government almost unlimited powers? By the War Measures Act brick can be changed into stone. What was the reason for non-interference in this particular instance on the part of the Government?

When such exactions are perpetrated can we wonder at the industrial and social restlessness in Canada? It is claimed that there are dangerous leaders, that Ithere are men who are agitators, that there are in this country-as was affirmed in this House this afternoon by the hon. Solictor General (Mr. Guthrie)-men who want to overthrow our established institutions. No quarter for them, is my advice. But, Sir, no quarter also for another objectionable, and not more desirable, party-the profiteer. Let us try to assist the honest endeavour of labour to gain in this country a better standard of life. This effort is commendable, and anything in reason that can afford a better standard of living, together with some of the comforts of this world, should not be denied the most important, after all, of the factors of production and wealth. It seems to me that if this condition should be reached, social strife would come to an end.
Mr. Speaker, after my Release, and as 1 entered Holland passing out of Germany, I experienced emotions which it is beyond my power to describe. It was on a spring day when nature awakens to a new life. I passed from a world of horror and strife into a world of peace and happiness. It was, as I said, on a day in spring when nature takes on new life. The luxuriant vegetation, the warbling birds, the fragrant atmosphere, the green pasture fields, the splendid herds, the placid streams, the happy children at play-everything appeared to me so beautiful and so entrancing, that I realized in the twinkling of an eye the immense chasm which separated me from a world of horror created by man and from which I had been transported to a world of happiness such as must have been created by God for the use of man. I could not resist the impulse of my soul, and a hymn of praise ascended to Heaven. I expressed the wish that an inspiration might come from above upon the two big elements in this social world who are engaged in conflict one with the other. I wished for an inspiration for the rich, for the employer, for the master, that he might be generous, and an inspiration for the one below, the one who toils, the one who suffers, the one who works, that he might be reasonable in his demands. Victor Hugo, in his magnificent study of Shakespeare, claims that there is a point where the spirit of man and the spirit of God meet and that point the great poet calls l'Tdeal. Comparisons are odious, but I will take that as an illustration only, and I will ask the House whether in this -cruelly tormented world the point may not soon be reached
where the mighty an-d the rich can extend the hand to the poor, to the working man, a point of contact where both hands shall feel the grasp of friendship and understanding, and where there shall be a movement of generosity on the part of the one above, and a movement of reasonableness on the part of the one below. This appealed to me as the cure for the ills from which society suffers at the present moment. It is nothing more nor less than the adequate apppli-cation of the law of Christianity.
This war has come to an end. Several forces have contributed to it-the economic force, the financial force, the military force, the moral force and the naval force. I refer to the naval force in particular, because I will ask you the favour of allowing me to narrate what I was a witness to when I passed from the shores of Holland to the shores of England. It was on the first day of July-Confederation Day. The moment of departure from the shores of Holland was unknown even to the passengers-; all that was known was that the passengers should embark upon the ships at 4 o'clock in the afternoon at Hoek Van Holland. There were five passenger ships laden with human beings, mainly women and children. The moment the passengers had boarded the ships all communication was cut off with the land. There we waited for a day, we waited for a night, and we waited again for half of another day. Then the five ships cut loose from the wharf. We came down the Maas river, the ships turned to the north, and followed the coast of Holland. Nowhere could be seen any ships to convoy and protect us against any attack that might come upon us.
Then when we had reached iScheveni-ngen the five ships headed for the high seas, and suddenly in the far distance a little -cloud of smoke was visible which grew larger and larger as we approached. Every one was wondering what it was, whether it was -a detachment of the German- navy or -a detachment of the British navy. But after a few minutes the news was spread over all the five ships that what we had noticed in the distance was the in-coming convoy- the convoy that had left the shores of England in the morning and was arriving in Holland. And then what a pageant was offered to our sight! This convoy which was- coming through the North sea-the field of operations par excellence -of the German- pirates-consisted of seven passenger ships -convoyed by seventeen war ships. When we came together, after a moment of apparent confusion, the seven ships in-

coming from England entered Dutch waters -the zone of security-and we were heading for the coast of England in single file preceded 'by a grim cruiser and having on each side of us eight torpedo destroyers., scurrying to and fro like hounds of the sea with a speed unimaginable. We continued until one o'clock in the afternoon, when we entered a field of floating mines, and there the British gunner was at work. These mines were visible at the surface of the water as little dark points, and the British gunner alter two or three shots revealed the fact that he had recorded a bullseye- a mine was exploded and a column of water shot into the air. Then we proceeded until at nine o'clock in the evening we noticed in the distance two big lights, which indicated to us the mouth of the Thames. Suddenly those sixteen warships closed upon us as in a movement of affection, and as we passed the line which united those two lights we felt that we were in a zone of security from which the German pirates were excluded. And then with blinking signals the seventeen warships turned about and started plunging into the night, into the tossing waves on another mission of protection and humanity.
That was, Mr. Speaker, one of the most impressive sights which it was ever given ' me to contemplate. The British navy has during this war played a wonderful part.
It has, indeed, saved the British Empire. And in times of peace the British navy is there. But to perpetuate the British Empire, to have it as we want to have it, a galaxy of united nations, one thing is of paramount importance, and that is that each component part should be entirely autonomous.
In the British Empire the law of autonomy should apply; in Canada, as between races and creeds, the law of toleration should find its application; in the social world moderation in demands from the employee and generosity in concession from the employer should prevail; and in the economic world production and economy should go together. These seem to me, Mr. Speaker, to be the stars that should guide Canada towards her glorious destiny.
Mr. FRANK S. SCOTT (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, it is well known that on the occasion of the Budget debate a good deal of latitude is allowed in the subjects that may be referred to. We understand the circumstances under which the hon. gentleman spoke 'this afternoon, and I rejoice upon those circumstances; but he will not misunderstand me when I say that I shall

not attempt, in the few remarks which I shall make upon this occasion, to follow him in all the subjects which he has introduced.
'He made reference to the 'Canadian Expeditionary Force to Siberia, and I may be pardoned, perhaps, for referring to that for ope moment. As I understand the situation that force was. sent from Canada after consultation with the British Government, and it was designed to operate upon the eastern front against Germany and against her allies, Eenine and Trotsky. As is well known, at that time the position on the western front was most critical, and it was recognized by the British military authorities that something should be done to bring additional pressure "to bear upon the German eastern front. For that reason the force was sent from the Dominion of 'Canada. But in connection with that the point which occurred to me was this, -that in the matter of autonomy at a critical time like that, if that western front had been broken, what would have been the position of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, and what would have been the position of the Dominion and of all the rest of the world.
Now I will pass on to matters in which I am more particularly interested. I listened with a grea-t deal of interest to the speech delivered yesterday afternoon by the chief financial critic of the Opposition in his reply to the Minister of Finance, and the criticism which I would make of the position taken by the member for Brome (Mr. MoMas-ter) is that he had given most careful consideration to this question, but entirely from a theoretical standpoint. While theory has its place and must always be considered, I submit that on an important question of this kind there is a great deal of the practical to be taken into account, and I feel that the member for Brome would have been very well advised, having reached certain conclusions from a theoretical standpoint, to get into consultation with some of the business men in the great city of (Montreal from which he com-es and to discuss -those conclusions before he brought them to the attention of -this House.
One of the first points that he -made in his speech was that owing to the delay in bringing down the Budget this session there was stagnation in some parts of the country, and that great loss of business had resulted. I cannot agree with him in that conclusion. I may point out, however, that as a result of the introduction of the low tariff, free trade resolution by

my hon. friend in this House on March 25 last, a great deal of doubt and uncertainty was created in the minds of the business people of the country and a great deal of real loss took place. Let me illustrate'. In the city from -which I come a manufacturer told me that his firm had prepared plans for a new addition to their plant, but that when the resolution of the member for Brome was introduced and the controversy which took place at that time went from one end of the country to the other, they felt that they would not be justified in going ahead with the extension, so -that it was held up-at any rate, for the time being.
This controversy with regard to the tarift seems to come up in this House with regularity. It certainly is not a new question in Canada; it is not a new question in the Motherland or in the United States. For a hundred years they have been, debating in the United States whether or not the fiscal policy of that country should be governed by free trade principles or by the principles of protection. During all these years, while the cause of free trade has not been without its advocates, the keen business sense of the American people asserted itself from time to time, and the United States, during a century of the most remarkable industrial development of any country of the world, has -stood fast by the policy of protection.
The member for Brome said that it always amused him when the advocates for protection asked where the revenue was to come from. I shall not refer at length to that phase of the question; for the sake of argument, we will allow that matter to take care of itself. But I wish to say a few words upon the policy of protection and to state what I believe to be its merits- because from business experience I believe it to be the policy which is in the best interests of the country. I shall take one or two lines of industry with which I am familiar and endeavour to outline what I conceive to be the working out of the policy of protection as applied to them.
The first industry to which I shall refer has seen its greatest development in the neighbouring province of Quebec. I refer to it because I have some personal knowledge of it, and because it has been singled out by the advocates of low tariff and of free trade as one of the industries that was not playing the game fairly and that was taking undue advantage of the tariff. I refer to the boot and shoe industry, which has been referred to by newspapers
throughout the length and breadth of the country as an industry that was taking an unfair advantage of the tariff. I have a number of extracts here; I shall not burden the House by reading them all. Perhaps the following will be sufficient to emphasize my point; it is from an editorial published in the Ottawa Citizen on April 10:
The American manufacturer sells a pair of shoes to the American retailer at $5; the retailer adds his profit and sells to the consumer. When the American manufacturer sold the shoes at $5 he miade his legitimate profit. The Canadian manufacturer makes the same quality and same priced shoe, but knowing that he is protected to the extent of a 30 per cent duty he adds that duty, of $1.5*0, to the shoes, and sells them to the Canadian retailer at $6.50 instead of at $5. Yet at $5 he would be making his legitimate profit. Now, who gets this " protection " money? Not the government. Not the1 Canadian retailer. Not the consumer. The money goes into the pocket of the Canadian manufacturer, and simply adds that much to his legitimate profit. Let us see how this workedi out in 1913.
Then ifoHows a statement of the importation of shoes and so on. That kind of propaganda has gone from one end of the Dominion to the other. But perhaps the newspapers are not to be blamed; there was a very good excuse for it. On March 25 the member for Brome introduced his resolution for free trade on certain articles and reduction of tariff on others. Speaking to that resolution, he said:
Now, the man pulls on his -boots. If they came from England they were taxed 22J per cent; if from the United States, 32J per cent,-and if they were made by a Canadian manufacturer I beg leave -to suggest that you will find their price was just a little under what they could have been produced for abroad and brought into the country, freight and duty paid.
His contention is that the Canadian manufacturer takes the American price and adds the duty of 37J per cent, and that is his price to the Canadian consumer. After all, Mr. Speaker, that is the basis of all this controversy. In the remarks which I am about to make, I shall endeavour to show that that contention is absolutely false and incorrect.
I said a moment ago that the newspapers were not to be blamed for carrying on propaganda of this kind, having regard to the fact that a member occupying the important position of the member for Brome, who is chief financial critic of the Opposition, and who comes from the great commercial city of Montreal, made a statement of that kind. The least that he could have done under the . circumstances was to have secured people

engaged in that business or made inquiries in some other way and found out the exact facts. As a result of the working of the tariff on shoes, what is the situation? Some years ago there was a duty of 25 per cent on shoes. In 1907, representations were made to the Liberal Government of that day that fancy shoes, or the higher grades of shoes, were being imported into this country, and that it was desirable to increase the duty to 30 per cent. The present hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), who was Minister of Finance of that day, took these representations into consideration, and on the higher grades of shoes he increased the duty to 30 per cent and on staple lines of shoes he left the duty at 25 per cent, where it is at present. What is the result of the increase in duty on fine shoes "to 30 per cent? Cer-tian American factories which had been doing business in Canada, paying the 25 per cent duty and shipping their goods in here, found, with the increase in the duty and the progress1 made by Canadian manufacturers, it increasingly difficult and well-nigh impossible to meet the competition and pay the duty, and the result was that in more than in one instance factories which had connections over here started branch factories in the Dominion of Canada. The first point I want to make is this, that if it had not been for that duty, those Amreican plants would not have moved to Canada. How does this policy of protection work out as regards costs?
Some days ago I wrote to the Canadian branch of one of the most successful shoe manufacturing concerns in the United States, stating: You should be in a position to know perhaps more than any one else just what there is in all this talk that we hear about the Canadian manufacturer taking full advantage of the duty, which with the war tax is at the present time, 374 * per cent. I asked him if he would give me the prices charged by his American plant and by way of comparison the prices charged by his Canadian plant, and I am going to give these figures to the House for its consideration. He gives me the prices on three classes of high grade shoes. On a tan calf bal, the United States' price is 57.50 as compared with the Canadian price of $8.25. The difference is, therefore, 75 cents, or an increase, not of 374 per cent, but of 9 per cent. On a gun metal bal, the American price is $7.15 as compared with the Canadian price of $7,60. The difference is, therefore, 45 cents, or an increase

of 6 per cent over the American price. On a vici kid shoe, the American price is $7.40 as compared with the Canadian price of $8.35, the increase being 13 per cent over the American price.
Just allow me to point out this difference: If the argument of our free trade friends were correct, that Canadian price of $8.25 would have been $10.30; that price of $7.60 would have been $9.85, and that price of $8.35 would have been $10.15. Then I am met with this question: Why, after all, should there be any difference? There is a difference in the price of those three articles varying from 6 to 13 per cent, and that difference is arrived at in this way: All hon. members know that we pay duty on our raw material. Since this war began we have h.ad a duty of 74 per cent on hides, and a similar duty on leather, and wherever these commodities have been imported from the United States the Canadian manufacturer must of necessity add that duty to the cost of his goods. We are told that our customs receipts amounted last year to about $150,000,000, part of which is taken up in the small difference to which I have just referred between the Canadian price and the American price on shoes. As an example, upper leather coming into Canada from the United States is subject to a duty of 224 per cent; patent leather, 324 per cent; sole leather, 25 per cent; cotton lining, 324 per cent. That comparison in prices is on the finer grades or the more expensive shoes. An investigation at the present time into the cost of shoes as between Canada and the United States on the more staple lines will, I believe, show that where Canadian goods are made from materials produced in Canada the prices will be just about the same; perhaps in Canada some will foe lower. I have here a statement prepared by the War Purchasing Commission with regard to the purchase of army shoes. The Canadian War Purchasing Commission kept a close record of the prices paid by the Canadian Government and those paid by the American Government. The United States Naval Department, in 1918, were paying $5.99 for shoes, while the Canadian Naval Department were buying shoes of a similar character for $5 a pair. Those were more staple shoes and made of Canadian material. I am not going to burden the House by reading this statement too much in detail, but in September, 1918, the Canadian Militia Department were buying 'Canadian pattern boots at $5.40 per pair, while the United States War Department were paying $6.45 for their pattern boot, and

their boot had no better wearing qualities than the Canadian, as they -permitted the manufacturers to use a lighter leather. Therefore, the conception that the Canadian manufacturer is governed by the duty in the selling price of his goods is absolutely incorrect.
There is another industry closely allied with the shoe industry, and I want to refer to it to-night, because it bears out perfectly my contention as to how the tariff has worked out and is going to work out when applied to Canadian industry. As hon. members all know, shoes are made upon wooden lasts, and the manufacture of lasts is quite an important industry. Some years ago lasts were largely imported from the United States, although we had some small Canadian factories. There was a duty of 30 per cent on lasts.
As the Canadian manufacturers improved their methods, American manufacturers found it difficult to ship their goods into Canada, and the result was that the best and most successful last manufacturers in the United States established plants in Canada. There has been a duty right along of thirty per cent on lasts. What has taken place? The price of lasts in the Dominion of Canada to-day to a shoe manufacturer is exactly the same as the price in the United States, which means that the manufacturer has taken absolutely no advantage of the duty. As I discuss these question with our friends from the West and elsewhere from time to time I sometimes hear this argument: "If we can manufacture goods just as cheaply in Canada as they can in the United States, what is the object in having a tariff at all? Why not do away with it?" On this very point I am going to read a statement made by the member of this House prior to 1911, on a motion to reduce the duties on agricultural implements:
My 'belief is that if this motion were passed we would strike a severe blow at one of the great industries of the country. I believe the International Harvesting 'Company in Hamilton would And it to its interest to close up its business, at least as much as is devoted to mowers and binders, and have them made at the American branch and bring them froim the United States. The factory in Hamilton is an American concern. With a moderate duty we have induced American capital to come into Canada and to establish that great industry, and after we have brought it in and established it Canada, I believe that if they were to pass this resolution that the Company operating that industry would find it profitable to close their. Hamilton factory and bring in the goods which they make in the United States.
