Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I had just concluded the reading of an extract taken from a speech delivered in 1907 by the then Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) on the importance of continuing the tariff. It seems to me that if it was important, from the standpoint of maintaining our industries that the tariff should be upheld at that time, the necessity for doing so is far more important now. I return again to the question why, if Canadian manufacturers are producing goods, as I know they are in a great many cases, just as cheaply as they are being produced in the United States, the tariff should be maintained. My answer to that question is this: We are living side by side with the greatest industrial nation in the world, a country which is a great deal larger and stronger than ours from an industrial standpoint, and a much richer country. What is the position of that nation at the present time? We know the the Government of the United States, and their business men and captains of industry, are reaching out to all corners of the earth in order that they may take advantage of export trade. Consider the close proximity of this Dominion to that great country; look at the great advantage that the American manufacturer enjoys with regard to the Canadian market. If the tariff that now exists between the two countries were removed it would mean the equivalent of adding to the market of the American manufacturer eight or ten additional states. Look at the strong position the American manufacturer already enjoys. Take almost any line of manufacturing and the tastes of the Canadian people are just about the same as those of the people in the United States. We read the same magazines that they do; they advertise at great expense, and if it were not for the present tariff the American manufacturer would be able to ship his goods into the Dominion and dump them here, and Canadian manufacturers, at least in but very few lines, would be unable to compete with him. The reason for that is that the industries of the United States take care of their own market. In so doing, all working charges, all overhead expenses, and all salaries are met. Open up the Canadian market, without a tariff, to the American manufacturer, and what will be the result. He can produce goods at a lower price and the charges which I have enumerated, having already



been provided for, he can quote for the business offering in this country much lower figures. Therefore, just as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) pointed out in 1907 that it was good business for the Canadian people to maintain the tariff, 1 contend that at the present time it is particularly in the interest of our _ people that we should follow the same policy. We have heard a great deal already in this debate about the great financial obligations that are burdening our people as a result of the war. In my opinion the only way in which Canada will be able to successfully meet these financial obligations in future is by increasing business and trade. Rather than consider at this time the reduction of the tariff, it occurs to me that we might better find out how we can encourage o-ur industries and develop our business so as to successfully meet our financial obligations in the years that are to -come. Great Britain had not been very long engaged in the recent war until she discovered that her great necessity at the outset was the manufacture of shells, -and she turned to Canada, to tlhe United States, to every country from which she could hope to secure supplies of shells. The Mother Country had only been a short time engaged in the -struggle when her public men realized that in a long, drawn-out encounter such as the war promised to be, even with the great wealth which Great Britain possessed she -could not carry on- the fight along these lines to- the limit that her adversary, Germany, could, unless she changed her methods. Why was that? It was because Germany was making her own -shells, spending the money within her own borders, and giving employment to her own people. Therefore, Mr. Lloyd George and the Parliament of Great Britain -soon realized that -if they were to be able to continue the war, maintain Great Britain's financial equilibrium, -and carry on as they should they had to establish great shell industries in- Great Britain, and they did so. It appears to me that, now the war is over, we in- Canada are confronted with exactly the same -conditions of affairs, from a business standpoint, as Great Britain was at the time to which I have referred. We have great financial obligations and in my-opinion the only way in which we can meet those obligations is by manufacturing and producing at home.
These are one or two thoughts in connection with that viewpoint that I would like to leave with the House to-night. I am not one of those who say that the tariff is a cure for all evils. I do not main-
I-Mr. Scott. 1
tain for one moment that there are not individuals who are taking unfair advantage of it. I do not say that the tariff at all times- w-orks out in just the way it should. We never saw any method of taxation yet that is perfect in its operation. Take the operation of the tariff in connection with the motor car industry. It does not appear to me that things are not working out in the industry just the way they should. Considering the scale on which the purchase of motor cars is carried on it is a great big burden on the Canadian people, and the quicker we find out some way of making these motor cars in Canada the better it will be from the Canadian standpoint. What is the situation in regard to the motor car industry? It is true we have so-called manufacturing establishments in Canada, but as a matter of fact they manufacture comparatively few of the parts -that go into a motor car. These parts are imported from the United States and the customs duty is paid on them. Well an-d good. It would be a great thing if these goods could he made right here in this Dominion so -that, instead of having an adverse balance of trade and an exchange rate Of 3 per -cent against us, such as we have at the present time, these things would be made right here and a new industry would be built up.
There is another industry that I would like to refer to along the same lines. Some years ago Parliament -put a duty upon sugar. As a result there was established in Canada, on a very small scale, what is known as the beet- sugar industry. In 1902 there was under cultivation in sugar beets in Canada an aggregate area of 2,000 acres. In 1918 the acreage had increased to 25,000. In 1902 the production of sugar was 3,000,000 pounds; by 1918 it had increased to
50,000,000 pounds. In 1918 the total consumption of sugar in Canada was 600,000,000 pounds. I am informed that during the year 1919 the beet sugar factories of Canada will produce one-twelfth of the sugar consumed in this country. If we had no beet sugar establishments here, and if we had to import all our sugar we would send out of Canada 57,000,000 that at the present time is being left in this country, while employment in agricultural production is being given by this industry to 1,500 men. Beet sugar agriculture is one of the most profitable agricultural employments that any man can engage in. I am informed that in the county of Kent, where that business is largely centered a man engaged in sugar

beet cultivation can clear $100 an acre, and that land values have increased there, as a result of beet sugar cultivation proving so successful, from $100 to $250 per acre. In 1918 the Dominion of Canada sent abroad in payment of her sugar bill $40,000,000. Is it not a proper thing for this country to have regard for a situation of that kind? What are we doing to bring about a condition under which 85 or 90 per cent of the sugar that we consume in this country will be grown and manufactured here? Are we going to make a big success of the beet sugar industry as they did in Germany? Germany took up this same proposition, developed the beet sugar industry, and as a result enriched her soil and placed herself in a splendid position as a country of agricultural production. If we do that we will have in Canada 250,000 acres devoted to the production of the sugar beet. This area will be in the highest possible state of cultivation, because it is a well known fact that the cultivation of the sugar beet does more to enrich the soil than any other crop. We would, I repeat, have under this culture 250,000 acres and our farmers would receive $27,500,000. This industry would give employment to thousands of men in our fields and factories. Instead of talking about revising the tariff, if the Government would try and encourage industries of this kind, we would be going about things in the proper way.
I would like to speak briefly upon the question of the business profits tax. I am rather inclined to think that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) will agree that this is not a very desirable method of taxation. I have heard that view expressed by men occupying prominent positions in this Government. When it was first introduced, I did not like it. I did not think that the principle was sound, but the war was on, and people after all were ready to assume pretty nearly any obligation they might bo called upon to assume as a result of the war. It may be that we are considering this as a war year. For that reason perhaps I should not too strongly criticise this tax. I do not know that the Canadian business man will object to paying that tax once more, but I submit that it is not a proper or a fair tax. I am going to take what may perhaps seem an extreme case to illustrate the operation of this tax; I am going to take a business with a capital of $100,000 and making $25,000 in profits. By careful management, by turning their capital over several times, I have no doubt, some businesses will be able to obtain that much.
210J
With a capitalization of $100,000 under the operation of this business profits tax your business institution would be exempt on $7,000, or 7 per cent on its capitalization; the tax takes 25 per cent of the earnings from 8 to 15 per cent on the capitalization; 50 per cent of the earnings from 15 to 20 per cent; and 75 per cent, or three-quarters of the earnings, over and above 20 per cent. Figuring that cut, the tax on a business making those earnings would be $8,250; if the business earned $50,000 instead $25,000, the tax would be $27,000. That is an illustration of what a man would have to pay who is carrying on an industry and giving employment to a great many people. I am going to contrast his position with the position of a capitalist who has perhaps retired from active business. He has secured a fortune of, I am going to suppose, $500,000. His income from that $500,000, properly invested, is $25,000. If he has invested his money in some ordinary security he will pay, I think, under this new income tax, about $2,800 or $3,000; under last year's income tax he paid considerably less. Now you see the difference. Here you have a man engaged in business taxed $8,000 if he makes $25,000, and taxed $27,000 if he makes $50,000; while the other man, engaged in no business-playing golf perhaps in the afternoon, with nothing at all to worry him -gets off with a great deal less; and if he is fortunate enough to have that money invested in Victory bonds he pays absolutely no tax.
The point I want to make is that no individual in this country wants to avoid paying his fair share of taxation, but that this is an unfair discrimination. I do not consider such a burden taxation; it is confiscation of a man's property. I know in my own district more than one manufacturing institution that has been borrowing from the bank more money than in ordinary times they ought to borrow, and now they have to go to the bank, to borrow still more money to pay their taxes. 1 submit that that is not a proper condition of affairs.
If you are going to have an income tax you can apply it just as you are applying it at the present time to a manufacturing or business firm and you can make that concern pay the tax the same as you make an individual pay. But I do submit that if we are going to have an income tax we ought to have it applicable to all people, and that a small part of the community should not be singled out in this way. I think it is a mistake from a national standpoint. There is no money of more impor-

tance to the people of this country than money invested in industry, and I maintain that this $40,000,000 a year that has heen taken from a few through the operation of this business profits tax has been taken out of industry, and that by far the greater part of it should have been left with the owners in order that they might extend their organizations and in that way build up the trade of the country.
Since I became a member of this House I have heard from time to time a good deal about the income tax, and I understood that when the farmers were liable to the tax everything would be perfectly satisfactory to them. Well, 1 do not know how the other members find it, but I am convinced that when the income tax-we have not really started to operate it yet-is in full operation, it is going to be the most unpopular method of taxation that ever struck the Dominion. As a rule the farmer goes to the bank manager of his county town about certain matters of business. The farmers of this country are going to their bankers to-day about this income tax, and my conversation with a number of country bank managers leads me to the conclusion that this income tax is not very well received by the farmers, and that they are more concerned about how they are going to get out of paying than they are about paying it.
The income tax as we have it at the present time is being paid by a certain class of people; by the salaried man whose salary is fixed and it is known just exactly what his earnings are; by the industrial worker, because the manufacturer is required to' make a return to the Government of just exactly what his men earn; and by the man that I referred to a moment ago, the man of wealth who has interest coming in from his investments. But in so far as the ordinary individual is concerned, the Government is not getting any income tax from him, and I do not believe that by any system we could work out the Government will be able to get a fair return of income tax from the people generally.
The neighbouring republic has been working on this income tax longer than we have. There are 6,000,000 farmers in the United States, and last year only 15,000 of them paid income tax. Does any one believe that when the war was at its height and prices for agricultural products were never so inflated, that out of those 6,000,000 farmers only 15,000 were liable to income tax? We have heard a great deal during the last year or so since the Democrats
tMr. Scott. J
came into power about the great change that came over the people of the United States on the tariff question. I admit that when the Democrats came into power some tariff reductions were made. But what is taking place in the United States at the present time? President Wilson before he landed in New York on his return from the Peace Conference sent a cablegram to this effect-I have not a copy of the message itself: We have to revise our tariff, and we have to have a tariff with some kind of teeth in it. Take the proceedings of the Ways and Means Committee of the House of Representatives right at the present time. They have been discussing the question, and the- views of the chairman are given in the following extract:
The importance of the home market is emphasized by Chairman Pordney of the Ways and Means Committee of the next United States Congress who has forecast a higher tariff for the United States. " I am not in favour," he says, " of chasing rainbows around the world to find a market for our surplus-which in amount is only about 7 per cent of our normal production-and at the same time neglect our home market and open the bars to the flood of goods offered us, made by the cheap labour of the world, to the detriment of the labouring people."
The first resolution dealt with by that Ways and Means Committee in the House of Representatives in the United States is in favour of an increase in tariff-I have the items here with respect to certain articles. The United States, as I said before six o'clock, have had over a hundred years of this tariff controversy. There have been times when they weakened upon this question-public opinion ebbs and flows-and when there have been changes of Government; but every time there has been a weakening of the tariff in the United States, bad times have followed. You may point out that there has been an exception during the last four years, since the Democrats came into power. But that is not a fair criterion, because the great war came on and all the energies of the industries of United States were directed to supplying the needs of Europe and of other nations of the world. But, make no mistake, the trade policy that has built up the United States will build up Canada.
I was present in this Chamber .the other day-I think you were present, Mr. Speaker, as well as most members of the House-and had the privilege of listening to an address delivered by a distinguished Canadian, Professor McLennan, who told us something of the work carried on by him and by others in connection with the efforts to meet the submarine menace. He told us

what could be accomplished by the application of science and research work to trade and to commerce, and he made inspiring references to the resources of this great Dominion. You will remember how he went from province to province and pointed out the great natural resources possessed by each. The great thought that he had for members of this Parliament and of the Senate was this: Faced as we are with this great debt and with the obligations resulting from the war, we have to look at things in a new way. His idea was that we had to call to our aid science and industrial research, and that we had to develop the industries of our country. I believe that is the policy of the future; that is the thing that we have to do. Suppose we had gathered around a table representatives of all the provinces, and suppose we were proceeding with the policy outlined by Professor McLennan. Suppose we had a report from British Columbia telling us of their great resources and suggesting how those resources might be developed; what would we th'ink if some representative from Ontario or Quebec said: That may be all right, but British Columbia is a long way off; we have no direct interest in the matter? If that view were taken we would not get very far, from a national standpoint. What would you think if the people of the Maritime Provinces represented that certain things should be done in order to bring about the development of that part of the country, and the people of Saskatchewan or Manitoba said: No, we are a long way removed from the Maritime Provinces; we have no direct interest in the thing? If we follow a policy of that kind we shall never get very far in a national way; but that is exactly what the Canadian people are doing in regard to this tariff business. We are looking at it from the sectional standpoint when we ought to be looking at it from the national standpoint. Only by having the national interest in view can we hope to bring about the proper development of this Dominion; of that I am assured.
I confess that as I listened to the remarks of the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) yesterday, I became just a little pessimistic, just a little depressed. He painted such a gloomy picture of the mistakes that had been made that I wondered whether, after all, we had done as well as we might have done. I have since had some time to think over his speech, however, and I am persuaded that, looking back over the past, looking back to the days when the National Policy was introduced and we began to develop our industries, and looking back over
events of the past five years in Canada, no man has any reason to be ashamed of Canada's record. There is in Canada too much minimizing and belittling of our national effort; there are too many class jealousies, too many cleavages. From now on, if we are to face the future successfully and meet the heavy obligations that confront us, we must look at these things from a different viewpoint; we must work for a common purpose. With our friends from the West we may have differences of opinion on these questions, but one thing is certain-we are all Canadians. There can be no doubt about that; the war has shown it, and it is only necessary that we should look at matters from the national standpoint in order that the future of Canada may be assured.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very attentively to the remarks of the member for South Waterloo (Mr. Scott), and he certainly ran true to form. He told us the same story that has been told by every other manufacturer-member and every other member representing the manufacturers during the last ten years, during which time I have been in this House.
The hon. member speaks about sectionalism. He does not have to go outside the boundaries of his own province for sectionalism; it does not exist in Western Canada. He is supporting the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White)-and he well might; he did not find fault with a single item in the whole thing. Why? Because it is a protectionist Budget, a Budget in the interests of the protectionists of this country, to which we, representing the farmers of Western Canada, object. I hope you will bear with me, Mr. Speaker, while I read from the Ottawa Citizen of June 6. In an editorial published on that date, the Citizen deals with the effect of the Budget. It says:
Sir Thomas White's latest Budget is likely to have one stimulating effect: it should cause the people of Canada to study their economic position in the world with an intense personal interest, more than ever before. It is a conservative Budget. High protectionism is still maintained as the fiscal policy of Canada. The Finance Minister proposes no substantial step towards, a low tariff policy.
It is true that the war tax of five per cent against British trade, and the 7J per cent tax: against the commerce of other countries, both taxes added to the tariff in 1915, have been taken off. But the tariffs are still maintained sufficiently high to promise no considerable reduction in the cost of living.
Further on, it says, speaking of the manufacturers and the loss of $17,000,000
I

which the Government promise to take off and which they are going to replace by an income tax-to which I have no objection:
When they-
That is, the people of Canada.
-paid 17 million dollars customs revenue, they also contributed about 51 millions a year to private protectionist enterprise, above necessary prices.
And further on it says:
The Government will still take about $130,000,000 from the people in customs taxes; andi protected interests behind the tariff will enjoy the privilege of adding about three times as much to prices of goods produced in Canada.
That is what I object to. I am not going to follow the advice of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton) and attempt to discuss the tariff scientifically, I am going to endeavour for a short time to discuss it in a common sense way. The Minister of Customs said last night that the tariff is only for a year. But I have heard the same story for at least thirty-five years. I have lived over forty-three years in Western Canada, as long or nearly as long as the Minister of Customs has. As a pioneer and as the son of a pioneer I have seen the struggle of the people in Western Canada. I have seen the farmers of that country besieged and put out of business by the machine men and horse dealers in the old days. I have seen men there struggle for years endeavouring to make a living for themselves and their families, and in the end the majority of those that I knew threw up their hands' in despair. I remember in October, 1895, the night that I, as a mere boy, attended a meeting in Emerson at which Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then plain Wilfrid Laurier, spoke. Wheat was then selling in the town of Emerson, which is in the county of Provencher, at 38 cents a bushel. I had bought oats myself at 11 cents a bushel, and to my personal knowledge these were the prevailing prices in Western Canada for many years. I remember one year in the month of March coming home from school and passing down the main street I saw a group of farmers congregated. They could hardly contain themselves because wheat that day had gone up to 50 cents a bushel.
Statements have been made as to the money farmers have made in Western Canada. I will deal with that matter first and come to the other later on. On a previous occasion, we had before the House, if I may be allowed to say, an amendment somewhat similar to the one that is now

under discussion. As a man who has lived in Western Canada all his life and who has been returned to Parliament three times by the people who know him best, I believe I know what is uppermost in their minds. I will not take upon myself, as some hon. members do, to speak for the whole West, but I will speak for the county of Provencher, and what is true of that county applies, I know, to the province of Manitoba. Some western members said that they could not support the amendment to which I refer because it would have meant the defeat of the Government. That statement is not correct; it would not have meant the defeat of the Government had they all voted for that amendment, nor will it mean the defeat of the Government should they all vote for the present amendment. And speaking for myself, the last thing I desire is the defeat of the Government at the present time. I am a good enough Liberal to wish that they would remain in power a little longer, to stew in their own juice. They can put up a little longer with some of the troubles and inconveniences that they are now undergoing. They were anxious for the position, and, as far as I am concerned^ they can find a way out as best they may.
I say the western members should have voted for that amendment. My position in this House is somewhat unique. Coming here in 1908, I came as a low tariff man; I have remained as such ever since, and I will remain as such as long as I am privileged to hold a seat in this House. I came here with Mr. Clifford Sifton, the one other Liberal member from that province, and he jumped the job. Later on I was elected on the question of reciprocity with the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Cruise) and he jumped his job, for he did not vote for the McMaster amendment. As far as the province oi Manitoba is concerned, I am alone. With this amendment before us, every rural member from Manitoba can vote for that which he .represents, and while high-brows may hold a different view, I hold that it is my duty while I am a member of this House to vote in accordance with the will of the people who sent me here and not to attempt to represent the whole Dominion of Canada. Perhaps that is a debatable matter, but that is the position I have always taken and the one that I am going to maintain. It makes no difference whether members from Manitoba were originally Conservative or Liberal, the people of that province, with perhaps the exception of the people of one constituency N

in Winnipeg, are straight low-tariff people, and there is an opportunity for members from that province to set themselves right before the people they represent. If they do not do so-and I understand some are not going to do so-that is their business, but at the next election the other fellows who come in will be those who will represent the views of the people. One of the members of the present Government, who was formerly a Liberal and who, I hope, is still a Liberal, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), speaking in this House, said that the people of western Canada are a unit on the tariff question; that they are all for a low tariff; and that is true.
Speaking from actual personal knowledge, let me say that farming in Manitoba has not been the paying proposition that some hon. members seem to think it has been. Not long ago, I heard an hon. member say that all the farmers of Manitoba and the other western provinces were clearing from $15,000 a year up. As a matter of fact, the history of Manitoba as regards crops is as follows: In 1912, to take as an instance the farm of Mr. Morrison who, at that time, represented the county of Macdonald, there were over 720 acres of wheat that he never cut, and thousands of farmers were in more or less a similar position; in many cases a binder was never put in the field. In 1914, throughout all western Canada, including Saskatchewan and Alberta, there was drouth. In 1916, there was rust, and in 1918-only last year -millions of acres of grain were destroyed by the prevailing high winds. That is every second year. The year 1915 was a banner year, but 1915 only partially made up for the losses of 1912 and 1914. There are, it is true, in western Canada individual cases where men, on account of high prices and being fortunate with their crops, made [DOT]some money. Some of them voted for Union Government and in some instances managed to keep as many as four sons and in others seven sons at home; but the average man who was either without help or had to pay the prevailing high wages did not make money. Therefore, I say that the farmers of western Canada did not make the amount of money that some hon. members would lead us to believe they did.
What is preventing the western farmers to-day from making money? First of all it is the high price of machinery; secondly, the high price of labour; and thirdly, the high price of lumber and cement. Wages have more than doubled.
For example, I have working for me a boy twenty years of age. Three years ago I paid him $40 a month. Last year I paid him $45, and $50 for the last five months of the year. This year I am paying him $70 a month and board, which is equivalent to $100 a month. Last year in the province of Manitoba, on my own farm, and on everybody else's for that matter, we paid for threshing oats and barley 12 cents a bushel, and 18 cents a bushel for wheat.
I want to say a word as to lumber. In the province of Manitoba, the oldest settled of the Western Provinces, the people are trying to go into the raising of live stock, and the first thing they run up against is the prices of lumber and cement, which are almost prohibitive.
As to. the reduction this tariff effects in the price of machinery, that does not amount to shucks; there is practically no reduction whatsoever. The reduction in the freight rate does not amount to anything either and we will not accept it. The first to benefit from the 71 per cent duty taken off coal are the railway companies. The deficit on the Canadian National Railway- and there will be a deficit-will be paid largely, and altogether so far as Western Canada is concerned, by the men who ship their grain over that railway. Freight rates have jeen boosted within the last year and a Y if. My grain cost 12 cents per hundred t<- carry. The rate was raised to 16 cents per hundred, and now the railways are asking for a further boost, and as usual, if they desire it very much, they will get it-. We contend that at this particular time more than at any other, the farmers of the West are not making the money that people imagine, and it is due to the high cost of machinery1, lumber, cement and wages. Wages is the highest item of all. This Government could very well put implements on the free list. That would have encouraged more men to go on the farm and stay on the farm, and would have done something towards reducing our national debt, which after all will have to be paid out of the natural resources of this country -the forest, the farms, the mines, and the fisheries. No encouragement whatsoever is given to the farmers in this Budget; that is not the intention of the Government. There are no objections from the manufacturers' point of view to these items being left as they are. I am sure that the Budget will not be accepted by the people of Western Canada. No matter how I or any other hon. gentlemen in this House may vote, the people of Western Canada have made up their minds that from 1878 down to the present time the manufacturers of machinery in this country have been unduly protected, and the protection has been wrenched from the producers of this country who have had to pay an undue amount of taxation to make up the revenues of the country.
The reduction on the cost of machinery by reason of the lower freight rate will not amount to anything whatever. I heard a man say the other day, who has farmed out West for many years, that he never objected to the price he received for his products of the farm, but the thing he objected to was the price he had to pay.
It is the price we have to pay
9 p.m. that we object to to-day. Everything that is used on the farm is taxed to the very limit. In 1912, the year when farmers' crops were destroyed by rain, binders were worth $160. This year they will be worth $248. Ploughs have doubled in price. Drills which cost $135 a year or two ago, now cost over $200. I bought a wagon a few years ago for $65; I bought another last November and had to pay $135. I objected to the price,- but I paid it. The dealer who sold me that wagon met me on the street about two weeks after and told me that the wagon I paid $135 for was now costing $168. The manufacturers of Canada last November or December fixed the price of the binder that will be used next August, and the same is true with regard to wagons and every other piece of machinery that will be used on

the farms of Western Canada, and Eastern Canada as well.
As to the national debt, the amount is beyond my comprehension, and, I think, of the majority of the people of this country. It is simply appalling. The Government, instead of making the farmer pay taxation on every implement he buys, might better have taxed some of the land in Western Canada held by speculators. One hundred million acres of land are held by speculators to-day, and I think I am safe in saying that the majority of these men do not live in Canada. When I was home at Easter a farm that a few years ago was raw prairie was selling for $50 an acre, or $25 an acre cash. The owner of the farm, an American citizen, had not seen it in twenty-two years. My neighbours and myself, and men like us, who have taken our chance in that country and spent our time and money in building roads and schools, in erecting churches and post offices, and establishing little towns, have increased the value of that man's land from, I suppose, $6 or $7 an acre to $50 an acre-$50 an acre cash is the market price in some sections now. Let the Government, as was suggested by Mr. Buchanan, writing in the paper of my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson), put a tax on the one hundred million acres of land held for speculative purposes by wealthy men. For all this land is held by wealthy men; the poor man cannot afford to speculate, he does well if he is allowed the privilege of living on the land and working it.
By imposing this tax the Government, of course, would ease the burdens of the taxpayers and the burdens of the producers in Canada; they would receive from that source money which would doubtless make them inclined to reduce the duty on agricultural implements and on the necessaries of life.
Now, so far as regards the farmers of Western Canada-and those of Eastern Canada also, because they are agreed on the matter-I maintain, that the proposition is an absolutely fair one. They say to the Government and to the people: Give us free agricultural implements with which to produce food, and make all food free. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the offer is unanswerable. They are not asking for any favours-they have never asked for any favours, and they do not want any now. What better or fairer proposition could they put before the people? As regards free wheat, that was granted by Order in Council in April, 1917, and it has now been made law. But we are not going to ship any wheat to the United States this year. The people there are pro-

ducing the largest wheat crop in the history of that country, wh.idh will amount to twelve hundred million bushels. Furthermore, I do not know that the United States would be very anxious to admit our wheat. The American Government has set a price on the wheat produced in that country, they have guaranteed tihe price, and they will see to it that their own wheat is disposed of before the Canadian wheat is allowed to be thrown on the United States market, because it will not be needed. The farmers of this country are standing for what might be termed a human, even deal. They propose to get it, and get it very soon. We are not worrying about the Government. They can keep the club that is wielded by the manufacturers and by some of the big interests of this country over the people for just so long; -but there will come a time when the people will resent it and resent it in an unmistakable manner.
In passing, I wish to say that there is a strong feeling of unrest in the province from whidh I come, and I charge the Government with being responsible for a lot of that unrest, outside altogether of the high cost of living. The statement which I make is this: The Government does not represent the people, and has not represented them since the 17th day of December, 1917. iMy ground for making the statement is that the Government was not chosen by the free people of Canada. That fact, together with the actions of the men who compose the Government, and the language used by the press of this country, the terrorism and the intimidations which were resorted to, the climax capped by the War-time Elections Act, prove to me conclusively that this Government does not represent the people. A great many of the people are of the same opinion, and that is one of the causes of the prevailing unrest, to say nothing of the high cost of living, and Ihe waste of public money that has gone on.
In the amendment which has been moved we are asking not only for free wheat but that the reciprocity pact of 1911 shall be given effect to, which will not only take in free wheat but also barley, oats, and many other articles. The American tariff of October 3, 1913, provides for a duty of fifteen cents a bushel on barley, six cents a bushel on pats, two and a half cents a pound upon butter and butter substitutes, and twenty per cent ad valorem upon cheese and substitutes therefor, one cent a pound on beans, and so forth. Free wheat alone will not satisfy the people of Western Canada; we want also a free market for everything we have to sell and
everything we need to buy, and we are willing that everybody else shall enjoy the same privileges that we do.
The agriculturists of Western Canada do not entertain-nor have I heard a single man at any public meeting, or anywhere else, express any such opinion-a feeling of antagonism towards the manufacturers of this country. The agriculturists of the West and of the East alike are anxious and desirous to see the manufacturers prosper in whatever lines they may be engaged. But the one thing the people refuse to do is to continue to pay the manufacturers that undue tribute through the taxation which has been levied for so many years past. The manufacturers of this country have, we believe, received protection at the expense of the common people for too long a period and have in fact enjoyed an undue amount of protection; and if, after all these years they cannot stand, so to speak, on their own feet, or on their own merits, and cannot compete with the manufacturers of other countries, as the grain-growers and the stock-raisers of Canada [DOT] have always been prepared to do, then as far as I am concerned they can shift for themselves-they have received all the patronage and protection to which they are entitled.
From the proposals that have been brought down by the Finance Minister, it would appear to me that the same interests that were out for the defeat of reciprocity in 1911 are behind this Government and behind this Budget. ..We see the Same Italian hand, the same leaders, and the same Government that defeated reciprocity in 1911. I charge the Government with having catered, and purposely catered, to the rich as against the poor. And the best proof of that is to be found in the way the Victory Loans in Canada have been handled. Those loans, to begin with are drawing interest at five and a half per cent, whereas a lot of the money invested in them was formerly drawing but three per cent. A lot of those bonds have been sold to people who can ill afford to pay for them, and who have in many cases defaulted payment. In other cases, by the most desperate efforts, the purchasers accumulated the money which they promised to pay. But where are these bonds now? The Victory Loan bonds of Canada are gradually getting into the hands of the very wealthy, and into the hands of the profiteers-the pets of the Borden Government and of the Union Government-and the Flavelles of Canada. That is where those bonds are go-

ing, and the common people of this country will have to>
pay the interest upon them. Nothing of any value has heen accomplished by this Government although it was heralded far and near as the best administration that ever existed, or would ever exist, in Canada. Instead of being a success, it has been an absolute failure from the day its members took office until the present * time, and no one knows that better than the Government itself. There are vacancies in the representation in this House from Prince Edward Island to the province of Saskatchewan, and yet this Government is afraid to hold one single by-election. Unless I miss my guess the present vacancy in the Cabinet will not be filled on a byelection either, unless some gentleman from the city of Toronto should be chosen as Minister of Agriculture. If the Government would accept a hint from me I would suggest that they choose as Minister of Agriculture the editor of the Orange Sentinel. I think he could be elected in the city of Toronto, hut he would not be elected for any constituency in Western Canada, and I doubt whether he would be elected for any seat outside of the city mentioned.
He (has not got to be elected under the law as passed last year.

No, he can just walk in. I have heard the statement made that all Western Canada supported Union Government at the last election. I understand from the last three or four hours that I have spent in this House, that a number of hon. gentlemen who were believed to be opposed to the Government are going to support it, but that is their business. The War-time Election Act, which should have been entitled " Thou shalt not vote unless thou votest for Union Government," was a big factor in returning the Union Government in'Western Canada.
I am going to mention something else that was a big factor in returning the Union Government in Western Canada. I remember, on the 29th of November, 1917, being called up by a friend of mine and asked how I was getting along, and about my chances of election which I thought were very good. He said: "As far as you are concerned, you can stay at home; the farmers of this country are going to elect you." It just happened that that night five or six others did the same thing and gave me the same encouragement. I watched these men very closely. There were those who said that there were farmers in Pro-
[Mr. Molloy. 1
vencher who were opposed to this Government but who were bound to vote against me because their sons were exempted, something that the Government had no right to do-If the law of the land was conscription, why should the Government exempt a man's son, your son or anybody else's son? And I know cases where farmers, who had four, five and six sons who were not conscripted. I know one farmer in particular in the county of Provencher, who happened to be one of the men who called me up. He had four sons at home during the entire four years of the war. He walked out of town last year with $85,000. He refused to give anything to the Victory Loan, to pay any income tax. The sons of a man with that amount of money could have gone to the war as the sons of other men went, and he was not the only one whose sons were permitted to remain at home. A large percentage of the people in Western Canada did not vote for the Union Government because they thought it woulcj be a better government. They were opposed to the Government but they supported it because their sons were exempted in a good many cases. Not all of Western Canada supported Union Government but if Union Government got support in Western Canada it was due largely to these things,-western farmers' sons being exempted, the War-time Elections Act., intimidation and fraud.
There is one other consideration in connection with the matter as far as farmers are concerned. In almost every district in Manitoba there are a number of Canadian-born farmers who had moved to the United States, remained there a certain length of time, and then come back. These, without exception, say that they are sorry, due t-0 the taxation which this Government is going to maintain, that they did not remain in the United States because there everything they require is much cheaper than it is here-their machinery, boots, shoes, clothing, fruit, canned goods and practically everything you wish to mention. Why should machinery, boots, shoes, clothing, fruit and so on not be as cheap in Manitoba as in the bordering counties of Minnesota and Dakota? If this Government were not controlled by the big interests we would have cheaper goods. As long as they are controlled by these interests the manufacturer will get his and the farmer will get his- but in another direction. The manufacturers will get all the assistance they require while the producers will be left to shift for themselves.

. I want to say a word to the hon. the Minister of Finance in regard to the Budget as it affects the people of Western Canada. The Minister of Finance can mail the Budget back to his friends, the same people who opposed reciprocity in 1911, namely, the mighty manufacturers, the Mackenzie-Mann bunch and the rest that go with them, and I am sure they will find it interesting reading. I would like to suggest another thing to the minister, and that is when he retires-and that will be very shortly-he write a book and entitles it, "The Four Big M's". The first "M" will deal with the Mountebanks who placed him in the Govei'nment and the big business people of this country who are looked upon as his discoverers. Second, he can deal with the Millions that he has unduly wrenched from the pockets of the poor people of this country. Under the third "M" he can deal with the Mountains of debt that he is going to leave to the people of Canada when he does retire, and which, I repeat, will be very shortly. Under the fourth "M" he can devote several chapters to the Misery he has brought about, the Mountains of debt and the waste of Millions by the Mountebanks of this country.

Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of this debate on what is undoubtedly the most important Budget ever presented to the people of Canada through its Parliament, my mind runs back to the war session of 1914. It was a very brief session, a matter of only a few days, but the country at that time was faced with stupendous problems, problems the extent and magnitude of which we did not then know. At this particular time we are again faced with immense problems. The problems of to-day are different, it is true, from the problems of 1914 and the subsequent years, but notwithstanding, there are problems just as complex and just as difficult of solution as were the special problems of those fateful years. Not only is that the case but, Sir, contrary to the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Molloy) who has just taken his seat, one of the main problems we are faced with is the immense debt. It is not due, as stated by the hon. gentleman, to the action of the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), but it is due to the events of the past five years. I think it is the duty of this House to set aside, in so far as we possibly can, alla personal animus and look these immense problems squarely in the face. It has been stated by a statesman who held one of the highest places in
our Empire, in presenting the Budget to the British House on an occasion fraught with difficulties, that the best way to overcome these difficulties was to look them squarely in the face. That should be the key note of this Parliament at this important session and with these momentous problems confronting us.
The other day the hon. member for Brome -who has assumed the role of financial critic for the Opposition-made a reference to the Minister of Finance which I did not think was worthy of the occasion, and, indeed, Sir, I am quite confident that his leader would not endorse it. Nor do I believe that it is becoming to the House or to one occupying the high position to which my hon. friend aspires, to deal frivolously or lightly with one of the noblest hymns in our literature. The hon. member used the paraphrase -which I will quote. He said:
.White moves in a most gracious way,
His blunders to perform.
And upon that he based his criticism of the Minister of Finance. If the hon. gentleman had been in his seat I would have directed his attention to the fact that one of the most important rules of the House is to refrain from naming an hon. member personally. I certainly think that he does not carry with him a very large degree of the intelligent opinion of this country when he refers to the Minister of Finance as having performed a series of blunders. I am of opinion that the minister's work during the whole period of his term of office, and more particularly during the most perplexing years that have just passed, has been marked with that high degree of ability and devotion to duty which will earn for him a high place amongst the statesmen of this country. What is the sense of casting what are really personal aspersions upon a minister who is at this time literally expending his very life blood in trying to carry on the financial affairs of this country? Personally, I wish to pay my tribute to the Minister of Finance for the excellent manner in which he has directed the important affairs of his office.
With the indulgence of the House I will deal with some of the criticisms of the hon. member for Brome. He speaks, of course, officially for hon. gentlemen opposite, and I invite them to consider with me some of his criticisms. Let us see if they have any merit. If they have any merit, it is due to the House to give them every consideration. On the other hand, Sir, there may he honest

differences of opinion between the two sides of this House as there might he between two individuals, and an expression of those differences may permit of some solution, or at least of an effort to that end.
My hon. friend very strongly condemned the Government for its policy of financing Rumania, and I presume-subject to correction-that he included in that the financing of other European countries. Let us see if this is fair criticism of the hon. Minister of Finance and of the Government. The facts are that a market existed in Rumania for our manufactured goods. There was a demand for goods; we had the goods to supply. Directly, as a result of the war, the credit of the average trader in Rumania was nil; not only that, but it was physically impossible to carry on business. His storehouses and places of business had been physically destroyed by the invading enemy, and there was a complete disruption of the financial and commercial affairs of the country. Therefore it was impossible for the manufacturer or for the trader in Canada to sell goods to the trader in Rumania, although the market was there. What happened? The Rumanian Government, recognizing the chaotic condition of the country, stepped in and said: "We will take the position of our traders for the time being until the country is reinstated in the ordinary conditions necessary to carry on business. And if you can assist us in the financing by making the nation a loan of $25,000,000, we shall be able to carry on." 60 instead of getting the credit of the individual trader, we got the credit of the nation. I have absolute confidence in the trading done under those circumstances^-for that implies absolute confidence, Sir, in the Minister of Finance and in the Chancellor of the Exchequer of the British Government, who has been our adviser in these affairs. That is briefly the situation, and it applies also to the loans to other countries which have been referred to. il argue from that that the criticism of my hon. friend was not fair, it was not sound ; and I venture to say that it does not receive the support of those manufacturers or traders who claim allegiance to the Liberal party. I am quite sure that as business men they will support the action of the . Government in this regard.
My hon. friend criticised very keenly indeed and deplored the bond issue in Canada of $1,500,000,000. He pointed out that it is a tremendous loan. Undoubtedly it is. He also pointed out that it is an exceedingly heavy burden, and he -made a comparison

between the landlord at home and the absentee landlord, and remarked that the former was sometimes more troublesome than the latter. But, Mr. Speaker, he refrained from saying that from one and a half to two million people, citizens of Canada, came forward and tendered this loan to the Government from time to time when called upon to do so. Out of our 8,000,000 population from one and a half to two million-1 have not the exact figures, but it is between the two I have named-came forward and helped their country to carry on. In my estimation that is a complete ^answer to the allegation that the moneyed men escaped taxation by subscribing to the loans.
What large institutions subscribed to the war loans outside of the individuals I have mentioned, who formed the bulk of the subscribers? It was the banks, insurance companies and other institutions. And whose money was it? Was it not the money of individual citizens which those citizens had entrusted to those institutions? We often refer to a bank or to an insurance company as if it was some individual who in his own right held the full capital of the institution, whereas it is held by hundreds, thousands, and in some cases tens of thousands of individuals. So when you analyse these criticisms you find they are based on this fact, that one and a half to two million people subscribed, and that even in the case of the large subscriptions they are again subdivided among a large number of individuals.
Now I come to my hon. friend's criticism of the tariff, and if I might be permitted, Mr. Speaker, without violating the rules of the House-and I shall, I think, keep within the rules-I would refer to a resolution proposed by the hon. gentleman some weeks ago-I think it was on March 25th-in which he gave expression to certain suggestions. I shall not read it, because that would not be in order, but I shall refer briefly to the views that he enunciated on that occasion, and then I desire to deal with the amendment before the House. He suggested at that time, in a resolution moved in amendment to the motion to go into Supply-it was really a want of confidence motion-first, that the most should be made of our natural resources. No one has objected to that; as a matter of fact, one of the objects of the proposals brought down by the Minister of Finance is to give effect to that principle. I will point out very briefly one or two facts in connection with this phase of the question.	[DOT]

We produce in Canada very large quantities of lead and copper, yet during all the years that we have been producing these things we have been shipping them to the American market in very crude condition- in the form of ore or of copper matte and spelter. For some years I have advocated consistently that these metals should be refined in Canada in order that a market might be created in our own' country for refined lead and copper and in order* that we might encourage the manufacture of these articles and their shipment to foreign countries in manufactured form. New Zealand, Australia, China, Japan, tlhe Singapore district, all import manufactured copper products, so that there is a large market for goods of this kind. Yet all these years we have been shipping the raw material to the United States and reimporting into Canada the manufactured articles of copper and lead. Now, the placing of a moderate duty on lead and copper will materially assist us in that regard; so I suggest that we are giving effect to the first point made by the member for Brome in his resolution of March 25.
Then he says that taxation should be imposed upon those best able to bear it. A moment ago my hon. friend (Mr. Molloy) offered some criticism of the business profits war tax and of the income tax. I am not going to debate the point, other than to say this: it must be admitted by hon. gentlemen opposite that we have taken a decided step towards imposing these taxes upon those, to use their own phraseology, most capable of sustaining the burden.
Then, the resolution of March 25 asks for reciprocal trade with the United States. But the next point is a rather striking one; they advocate the repeal of the five per cent war tax and the seven and a half per cent war tax. Have we not done that in the proposals which are now before the House? The five per cent war tax in respect of the British preference has been completely wiped out; the seven and a half per cent war tax has been wiped out in respect of something like two hundred articles. Is this not a decided step towards meeting the views of my hon. friends as expressed on March 25? Yet we are told in the resolution now before us that the action of the Government has been entirely unsatisfactory. What will satisfy hon. gentlemen? What do they want? We meet them, as it were, half way; yet we are told that the proposals of the Government are entirely unsatisfactory.
Then, we were asked on March 25 to put on the free list staple articles of food. We have done that. We have embalmed, as it were, in the statutes of Canada the Order in Council of a few years ago, virtually meeting the requirements of the reciprocity pact of 1911, without doing so at the dictation of the Washington government.
The next point suggested was with regard to agricultural implements, and so on. Just at this point I invite the attention of members of the House who differ from the Government to the phraseology of both resolutions-the resolution of March 25, and the motion now before the House. On March 25 the member for Brome, in his request with regard to farm implements, and so on, suggested that anything done should be without derogation from the provisions of paragraph (b) of his resolution. What is paragraph (b)? It is that the offer of reciprocity contained in the reciprocal trade agreement of 1911 should be accepts ed. In other words, the hon. member says to the western members on this side of the House: we will give you free implements- and he leaves that impression on their minds. But, tucked away in the phraseology of the resolution, we find words to this effect: "subject to the provisions of the reciprocity agreement." In other words, he intended to limit any concessions made with regard to the tariff to the reciprocity agreement. I submit that the provisions of the schedules placed before the House by the Minister of Finance meet that situation practically in its entirety.
Then he went on to request substantial reductions in the tariff. I invite the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite, and also of hon. gentlemen on this side who seem to think that the Government did not go far enough, to these words: "having regard always to the requirements of the public revenue" and the affording of "reasonable opportunities" for adjustment, and so on,-he would reduce the duties. That was in the resolution of March 25. In his resolution of to-day he use3 language a little different, but almost the same. He proposes a general reduction in the tariff, "as may be expedient and just to all concerned." I repeat that I invite an examination of this language. What does it mean? My hon. friend who preceded me, (Mr. Molloy), said: We want a free market; we want free agricultural implements; we want free this and free that; and we intend to have them. But where is he going to get them? He certainly is not going to get them from a government of which the hon. member for Brome may

be Finance Minister, because that hon. gentleman, officially representing his colleagues in this House, on two important occasions-once in moving an amendment to the motion to go into supply, and again in moving ah amendment to the Budget- uses the language to which I have directed attention, " having regard to the requirements of the public revenue." Is that not exactly what the Finance Minister is doing to-day-trying to face Canada's enormous debt and at the same time to make substantial reductions in the tariff? It is to be noted that the Finance Minister did succeed in making substantial reductions in the tariff, in spite of the necessity for revenue, and also in meeting the demands of hon. gentlemen opposite in that the added taxation is imposed upon those who are best able to bear it. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, in all reason, if we have not met their views as expressed a few weeks ago, almost in their entirety? As a matter of fact, in some respects we went beyond what they had hoped.
So much for that phase of the question. But the member for Brome did not stop there. He went on to blame the war upon protection. He said he believed the great war was due to two great, " and, as they have worked out, evil principles,"-imperialism and protection. I ask the hon. gentleman, did the fact that Great Britain was a free trade country keep her out of the war? Great Britain could have kept out of the war quite easily, but she did not do so, because it was not a war in which the issue was protection, free trade, or taxation; it was a war precipitated by the violation of solemn treaties, and it would not have made any difference whether we had protection or free trade; we had to take part in this war or lose our status as a nation.
Then, my hon. friend says that free trade is the panacea for all ills. I quote from his remarks:
I cherish the opinion that if the international gospel preached and practised by .great apostles of free trade, Cobden and Bright, had been followed by the rest of the civilized world, this war	would not have happened.
Let me call your attention, Sir, to his argument. He is presumably suggesting to the country that the party to which he belongs and for which he spoke on that occasion officially were standing for free trade. What does he say? He says that free trade would be possible had it been followed by the rest of the civilized world. That is quite conceivable. I confess that there is much in the theory of free trade

that has attracted my attention for many tears, but here is the stone wall to which I have always come in debating or reasoning this policy of free trade, namely, that as long as there is another nation which exercises what is termed the selfish policy of protection, so long will you be interfered with in the freedom of trade. That, of course, is a maxim that you cannot, perhaps, apply generally, but it certainly applies* in a country like Canada, and it applies in a manner that you cannot escape from, as is demonstrated by the very language of my hon. friend from whom I quoted a few moments ago. His lang'uage in both resolutions was to the effect that he proposed reductions in the tariff if expedient, having due regard to those interests, and I say that is made necessary by the fact that we are alongside of a nation of 100,000,000 with tremendous capabilities of manufacture, and a density of population making her market so great that our manufacturers cannot hope to compete with hers, at least, for a great length of time.
Let me briefly bring to the attention of the House the condition of Canada as it affects this policy. The fiscal policy of a country is one or other of two-either free trade or protection. If the policy he that of protection it may he a moderate protection. Nevertheless, you are confronted with the choice of one or the other. We have in Canada a very wide diversity of interest. On the extreme West we have British Columbia with its mining, timber and fishing. In the middle West, you have the three Prairie Provinces, so far as the settled parts are concerned 'almost an entirely agricultural population. But in the northern sections of those provinces, you have huge natural resources in the nature of oil, coal and other minerals. But when you come eastward into the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec, what do you find? You find not only large agricultural resources, but stupendous water-powers which twenty-five, forty or fifty years ago meant little but picturesque scenery. To-day those waterjpowers are measured by horse-power; they are measured as units of energy, capable of producing tremendous power for manufacturing concerns. While Ontario, perhaps, at the time of Confederation and for many years after was not fitted to compete with the coal areas of the Eastern States, because industry depended upon the presence ol coal for the development of steam energy, with the development of electrical machinery and power, Ontario, and Quebec in particular are destined to become among the

greatest manufacturing centres of this continent. This, however, cannot be brought about in a day; it is not something that' can be evolved over night;, it is a process of time. What has been the policy of Canada under the governments of Sir John A. Macdonald, of the late and revered leader of the Opposition, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, of Sir Robert Borden and under the present Union Government? The policy .has been a continuity of one idea, namely, to give an opportunity for the utilization of those great natural resources in the way of industrial development in order not only to develop the one great basic industry of agriculture-and that is desirable-but to develop those other industries the combination of which go to build up a great nation and people. For after all, history proves, beyond all per-adventure, that the trading nation, the nation that can send its goods into and meet and trade with other countries is a nation which is going to rise to the highest standard of civilization. That has been history repeated over and over again, and I shall not weary the House with illustrations. Therefore, I say that with our wonderful resources of agriculture, mining, lumbering, fishing and manufacturing, Canada is most fortunately situated to build up such a nation and people. I said a moment ago that we were faced with the alternative of one of two policies-free trade on the one side and protection on the other. Protection is capable of being moderate. You can have a high protection, such as Germany and the United States have, but we do not believe that is desirable. We on this side believe that a fair, decent protection, to enable our industries to get solid footing and to compete with the great country to the south, with its intense industrial life, is the type of protection we should have. We believe that this carried out in a moderate and sane degree is in the best interest of the country. On the other hand, I ask my hon. friends opposite this question: Are they in favour of free trade? I am reminded at this point of the words of their leader (Mr. McKenzie), an hon. gentleman who has distinguished himself during the past few months in filling the very difficult position in which he found himself so suddenly and unfortunately placed. That hon. gentleman the other day stated in the House what in his view was in the interest of Canada, and it was not free trade. My hon. friends opposite must frankly, if they would so address themselves to the House, say that it is,, to say the least, a partial free
trade. What difference is there in the terms? Moderate protection and partial free trade are synonymous terms; there is no difference between them, and well do hon. members opposite know that. I would invite the attention of hon. members who have'a faint hope that it may be possible to introduce a complete free trade policy in this House and in this country, to the language I have repeated on more than one occasion to-night of the hon. gentleman who represents the financial policy of the Opposition.
The other evening my hon. friend (Mr. MoMaster), in referring to the high cost of living, used two phrases, and again I take from his own mouth what I consider to be a complete answer to the criticism that he has hurled at this Government On page 3365 of Hansard he is reported to have said that the high cost of living was due to the scarcity of goods. He is absolutely right in that. The Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) described that situation to us at greater length than the hon. member for Brome did, and for some days now we have been sitting as a parliamentary committee studying the high cost of living, and every witness who comes before us impresses upon us that one fget, that the great fundamental, underlying cause is the scarcity of goods. Without labouring the question, as it has been reiterated so often, we have millions and tens of millions of men taken out of productive life and used in other lines, leaving a shortage of labour in the civilized world. My hon. friend knows that; he enunciates it as his reason. He says that the high cost of living is also due to an inflated currency. This' we know, and inflated currency is not confined to Canada, nor to this continent; it is common to the civilized- world; Great Britain, France, Belgium, Germany, Austria, Norway, Sweden, Russia and the other nations of Europe have very much inflated currencies.
Perhaps I should not have included Norway and Sweden. This is owing to world conditions; it is one of those peculiar phenomena known to finance. The high cost .of living is due to scarcity of food stuffs, goods and so forth, and to an inflated currency. How does my hon. friend propose to remedy this? By reducing the tariff as it may be expedient and suitable to those who may be affected. That was his answer; you could get nothing else out of his speech but that. " As it may be expedient." That is an intimation to the manufacturers that should hon. gentlemen opposite happen at some future time to come into power the manufacturers need have no

fear, because their interests will be carefully studied before there is any reduction. So those of my hon. friends who are interested in manufacturing and may have felt a little anxiety should take heart; there is nothing in my hon. friend's amendment to make them anxious. His proposals are simply a repetition of the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite in the years that have gone by. I congratulate them upon it, but I do think it would be better to be frank about the matter and say exactly what they mean.
Let me draw the attention of the House to what we have done. We do not say to the people that we propose to reduce the tariff as it may be expedient; but we have reduced it. We have placed on the Table lengthy resolutions reducing duties in a very marked degree, to the extent of some $25,000,000 of revenue at least. We may not have gone as far as some extremists would like, but we have given these reductions. We do not say in camouflaged language that we will make reductions as it may be expedient after due consideration. We say that we have studied the situation, have estimated the amount of revenue that is necessary to carry on, and have succeeded in devising a scheme for getting revenue to replace the amount that will be lost in duties, through the positive and definite reductions we have given. We say to the people of this country: We have to increase your taxes. I am quite sure that the leader of the Opposition, when he speaks in this debate will say something to this effect. He will not talk nonsense and say that he is going to reduce taxation, but will tell the people:	"We have a big
national debt consequent upon the war, and Canada's part in that war. That debt has to be faced, and the people of this country will have to pay heavy taxes for years to come." I am certain he will face the facts in that way, and that is what we are doing. We say we must raise the revenue whether it is pleasant or unpleasant, but we also say this: We look into the future and have absolute confidence in Canada's ability to rise to the magnitude of this.task. We believe that Canada is able to bear the burden, and will bear the burden, but in placing that burden upon the shoulders of the people we are considering the best and most just method of distributing it. , We have placed a larger burden upon the shoulders of the rich than upon the shoulders of the poor. In the resolutions which are now before the House, and which we on this side, generally speaking, support heartily, we have reduced the cost of living

to some degree at least, and we are endeavouring to find better and more effective means of reducing it. We have done our best in that regard. We have laid the burden of taxation very, very largely upon the shoulders of those best able to bear it.
A word on one or two other points before I sit down. I wish to impress upon the House the importance of the very much criticised bargain, so-called, made with the railways regarding freight rates. I have been trying for a great many years, so far as my feeble influence goes, to secure some reduction in freight rates, and I have found it a very difficult task. The freight rate question is a very important one. The Minister of Finance has succeeded in securing a substantial reduction in freight rates from eastern Canada to the Prairie Provinces. I have one thing to ask of him now. I invite his attention to the desirability of reducing commodity rates from the Pacific Coast to the Prairie Provinces, and from the Prairie Provinces to the Pacific Coast. Without labouring the question, I will put on Hansard this fact: Up to about ten years ago a merchant in Vancouver could ship goods as far east as Golden, about 450 miles distant, at the same cost that a merchant in Montreal could ship the same articles to the same point, a distance of 2,600 miles. In other words, ten years ago we used to be able to ship 450 miles as against 2,600. That has been reduced until to-day a merchant in Vancouver can ship as far east as Calgary as against the Montreal rate, or 600 miles against 2,300 or 2,400. Some
10 p.m. articles we can ship as far east as Begina, or 900 miles as against 2,000 miles. I state these facts merely for the purpose of asking the Minister of Finance and the Government to make an effort to extend this reduction on commodity rates to the West, because it would materially and decidedly assist in reducing the cost of goods to the Prairie Provinces.
I have this one further suggestion to make: Not only the Government but this Parliament should address itself to the development of the immense natural resources of this country. In eastern Canada, in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, as well as in the province of British Columbia, there are immense deposits of iron ore. There are also throughout this country tremendous deposits of copper, lead, zinc and silver. These are remarkably rich sources of revenue for the country, and I believe that any capital wisely expended on the development of these resources will bring splendid returns to this Dominion.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I have heard again and again gentlemen on the floor of this House casting reflections upon the province of Quebec, not only during this session, -bult for many years past. My hon. friend, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), on April 9th last, speaking about the slackers and evaders in the province of Quebec, made the following comparison: " A father has five boys in his home, all good strapping, sound lads; he is attacked by a bunch of bandits over night and, when the old gentleman calls for help, four out of the five sons only need to know (that the father is in difficulty and needs help to get them to the spot. But the fifth lies in his bed upstairs and says: Let the old man and the other boys fight it out."
The hon. member for Brantford went no further. He 'should have informed us whether the fifth boy had been treated as the others had been. I say that we, the people of the province of Quebec, who are looked upon as slackers, as evaders, and who are being thus treated by the English-speaking people of Canada,
