The participation of the counties of the province of Quebec in the war has often been referred to in this House, I often noticed that my hon. friends to your left, sir, endeavoured to show that the soldiers from their constituencies had cast their ballot in other counties. As far as I am concerned, I do not complain on 'that score.
I do not know the exact number of soldiers who have enlisted in our county-I may say that I did not insist upon recruiting-but I know that three soldiers did cakt their ballots overseas for the county of Laprairie-

Napierville. I cannot complain, as I have taken 33 and i of the vote. To tell the truth, with such opinions, as I have frankly given expression to in this House, I never believed that I could get any soldiers' votes. Ye't I have taken one-third of the military vote in my county, and I am quite satisfied.
I was rather amused to hear hon. gentlemen, on the floor of this House, refer to our marine and militia. So far as I am concerned, I should like my hon. friends to stop talking about our navy and our militia, because when a -country is bankrupt it can no longer do anything in that direction, and it behooves that country to let alone those matters for a while.
The people of this country are disgusted hearing all that talk about shipbuilding and militia matters. Those who travel a little, see in the large centres, Ottawa, Montreal, and aboard the trains, many young soldiers who apparently never were wounded-and so much the better for them-who are still wearing the uniform. At a time when farmers are lacking labour for production 1 wonder why the *Government should keep those soldiers idle in the Large cities, and thus waste the money of the country. Officers are thus allowed to strut about with gold lace and to live in idleness. We have a good many of'those officers walking around in uniform, who get 7 or 8 dollars a day and their living expenses, I believe, in first-class hotels. And both political parties apparently wink at all that. I have condemned in the past both political parties as to our participation in the war and unfortunately, they do not seem to be willing to hack me in order to put a stop to what is actually taking place in the country; for soldiers are still to be seen, at every street corner, at all hours of the night. And yet we are at peace. The war came to an end on November 11th last, or at least, the armistice has .been signed and peace will soon be concluded. Again, I ask, why so many soldiers?
But, brushing aside for the present that question, I now come to the speech of the hon. the Finance Minister. The hon. minister on the 5th of this month, told us that our national debt, in March 1920, will stand at no less a figure than $1,950,000,000 or in round figures $2,000,000,000. The minister always shows us the net. debt. The net debt does not mean much to us. I had rather be told the gross debt. At all events, what I am concerned about is the gross debt of a man, of a government, of a municipality, of a company. Let us take the case of a farmer, for instance-I am speaking of mat-

ters I am familiar with-who owns a good farm which is mortgaged to the extent of $4,000 or $5,000. Aeccording to the Minister of Finance, that would be the farmer's net debt. But if he owns the grocer, the butcher, the baker, the blacksmith, $2,000, that must be added to his net debt:	His
debt, will then be $6,000. Now, the minister's accounting is apparently similar to that of the farmer whose farm is mortgaged, but who does not say: "I owe $2,000 more." No, Mr. Speaker, a country's actual debt, is its gross debt.
I tried to-day to get the "Official Gazette." In the past, the actual debt was to be found there every month. There was a page which gave the assets and liabilities. I do not know whether it was the hon. Minister of Finance who prevented it, but for some time the public debt has not been mentioned therein. I really believe the hon. Minister of Finance must be somewhat ashamed to show it because it is enormous. However, if I remember .rightly-speaking from memory -in the month of April last, the gross debt of Canada amounted to $2,682,000,000, in round figures, and the net debt, on the same date, was twelve hundred and odd millions of dollars. . If $300,000,000 have been added to it since, then I can assure you that the gross debt must have reached, if it has not .exceeded, three billions. The Minister of Finance may not understand my remarks; I regret it, but he may read them later on. In the .same column which gives the net debt, the assets of the country are shown to have been $1,243,000,000 in the month of April last. I ask the Minister of Finance what these assets are worth. How much hard cash could he get. to-morrow in exchange for the $1,243,000,000 of assets which he had in the month of April last.
I surmise that funds have been advanced the British Government for ammunition, for provisions of all kinds and that, as a set-off, the British Government have' paid for our men overseas, for their maintenance, for their food, for the military stores spent upon the battlefields-which we shall have to pay for because we entered the -war, as some hon. members on the other side said, so as to pay for everything. Very well, but it is expensive. Now how much is debited to England and is a part of our assets, and what constitutes the balance of those assets? I understand it is money loaned to railways, to Mackenzie and Mann and others. We also have the railway, it is true, but that part of the assets is not worth a cent in my opinion. Then,

so as to be able to re-sell for $24 or $25. And those gentlemen have the ear of the Government, they are 'all powerful and everything goes on as well as 'possible with them.
Those are the people who make and unmake governments: hands off.
I am much less 'Concerned about the fiscal question than about the rights which we have in this country. I have always been a free-trader, and am still a free-trader, because I know that those manufacturers who are always clamouring for a high protectionist tariff only aid at rounding off their fortune. They are in their right in demanding an increase in the tariff, but they are no more in earnefst than the hon. minister was in 1913, when the 'Bill for giving dreadnoughts to Great Britain came up for discussion before the House. The right hon. Prime Minister then declared that warships could not be built in Canada. Mr. Churchill had cabled to him from England that we were too backward in shipbuilding in this country and 'that it would take fifty or perhaps seventy-five years before we could undertake anything in that line of business. Then the war broke out and we did build warships. INow, when manufacturers come and tell us that we cannot turn out, agricultural implements as they are making them in the United States; when they tell the Minister of Finance that in order to protect them, 20 or 25 per cent duties have to be imposed, I do not take any stock in their sincerity, and if the minister does believe them, 1 am bound to say that he is very credulous. No, sir, the protective system was devised to rob the people, and I use the word robbery because that is the only word that I can think of to express my idea. Protectionists may well be likened to thieves who steal apples in an orchard. While one shakes the tree his pal picks up the apples on the ground and drops them into the bag. Let me add that in their work, the protectionists have the hacking of the Government.
See what is happening in the United States with their high tariffs. Some individuals in that country have piled up colossal wealth, hundreds of million dollars. Can a man live long enough honestly to amass such a fortune? The span of life for a business man is from 30 to 40 years at most. Dare you tell me that it is pQssible for him honestly to pile up hundreds of millions? Surely not. 'He piles up those millions because he has the backing of tihe Government who lets him plunder the people by preventing foreign competition. That is what you [.ST. Lam:tot. ]
call protection. Protection makes the consumer pay for his goods three times what they are worth.
Give the people of this country absolute free trade-that is what I advocate-and free trade will give you honest governments. When you directly tax the consumer, he knows what he has got to pay, but when you tax him indirectly, as he is being taxed today, through customs duties, you make him pay unawares four or five times more than through direct taxation.
Should I go and tell the people in Lap-rairie-Napierville: "We are going to remove the duties and impose a tax of $20 per capita." What would the farmer say. "My dear sir, what do you mean by doing that? Are you crazy?" Yet he is paying now, through indirect taxation $20 per capita and the increase in price given to the commodities 'by duties ranging from 25 to 30 per cent, which, in many cases, doubles the sale price. And not only does he pay the duties, but he pays four or five times more for his goods.
(Let me tell you, before resuming my seat, that I am interested in that reciprocity question, but I am still more interested in the well-being of our'Ontario brothers. Western Canada is becoming Americanized. The Ontario imperialists who wanted to save the Empire at any cost, are now bending their efforts towards destroying it. Canada is actually in the same state as the town of Maisonneuve, at the time of its annexation to Montreal, in bankruptcy. Personally, as a Quebec man, I depreoate it; but our Western friends are clamouring for secession from the rest of Canada, because ithey look unfavourably upon the stand taken by the Ontario high protectionists. And later on they may say: "We are drifting towards the United States \" I deprecate such a stand, but as I already said that is bound to happen. What should the Ontario people do? Let them fraternize with the Quebec people; let them do away with the 17th school regulation and allow our French-Oanadian children to attend French-Oanadian schools. After all, I believe that the Ontario people are not more wicked than other people and in aspersing the Frenoh-Canadians, and reflecting upon Sir Wilfrid Laurier, they only aimed at remaining in power. Mr. Speaker, I have spoken at greater length than was my intention at the outset, but it was because I wanted to clearly de-fine my position.
